Remove a step when its useful work can go with it. The best objection to this rule is that almost any delay can acquire a respectable explanation once the person defending it is asked. A leader has to test the claimed function, not reward the explanation.

The booking number used to be typed twice.

A customer request entered one part of Northline's software. Someone then copied the relevant details into the system dispatch used. The two records could disagree, and an amendment could arrive in only one of them. Nobody defended the arrangement as good design. It had become part of the day.

Thomas replaced duplicate entry with a shared record of approved booking details. Sunder checked that amendments reached dispatch and interrupted transfers remained visible before they removed the second typing step.

Shaun's service team used the recovered capacity to finish the backlog of recurring customer problems Peter had already protected time for. By the end of the agreed fortnight, each of those cases had an answer or a named next action communicated to the customer. The work happened within paid hours. New problems would still arrive, but the old list was no longer being carried from one week to the next.

At Northline, clearing the backlog changed the next allocation decision. Peter released a defined block of service-team time for the workshop investigation, while keeping ownership of newly arriving customer problems clear. He could now fund the next piece of work from capacity that had been observed in use, rather than from the demonstration's promise of saved hours.

The call they stopped making

For a week, Sunder stopped making the call.

It was not a protest. Peter had asked him to examine which parts of dispatch coordination Northline still needed now that more information was visible in the system. Sunder had agreed to replace one daily call with a shared view of the relevant bookings. The service team could see what dispatch could see. There seemed little reason to repeat the information aloud.

By Thursday, an urgent request was competing with an existing reservation. The booking system showed the conflict correctly. Northline had already fixed the defect that once allowed two ordinary bookings to claim the same space.

This was a different question: should the company move the existing customer's collection to accommodate the urgent one?

Shaun had told the urgent customer he expected dispatch could make room. Sunder had asked the service team to establish whether the existing customer could move. Each was waiting for the other to finish a decision they used to make on the call. In the meantime, the urgent customer had understood Shaun's expectation as an agreement and stopped looking elsewhere.

When Sunder found him, Shaun pointed at the shared view.

“The conflict is there. I thought you were moving the first job.”

“Can that customer move?”

“I haven't asked yet.”

The information had arrived. The decision had not.

By the time they tried to settle the two requests, no comfortable remedy remained. Northline kept one promise through an expensive rearrangement and negotiated a change to the other. The call had occupied time; its absence now occupied people.

Peter had been right to question the call. He had mistaken its visible output for its whole job.

What a managerial activity contains

Middle management is an easy target when information becomes easier to obtain. If a system can summarise progress, answer a routine question and show the state of work, why pay someone to transmit those things up and down an organisation?

In some cases, there is no good reason. Reports are assembled because they have always been requested. Meetings distribute facts already available elsewhere. People seek approval for decisions that fall within rules everyone understands. Removing this work can improve both the business and the jobs of the people doing it.

But a managerial role may contain other functions alongside transmission. Behind the report may sit an exception interpreted before it became a complaint, a choice between commitments that could not both be kept, a misleading measure corrected or a resource obtained for a team that could not secure it alone. Those contributions are less visible than the report. Removing it can remove them by accident.

The useful unit of analysis is therefore the function, not the layer or title. Ask which decisions the activity changes, which conflicts it resolves and where those functions would move if the activity disappeared.

Sunder's call had transmitted information. It had also established priority when the day's requests could not all be satisfied. The new view replaced the first function. Northline had not explicitly replaced the second.

The shared view was a genuine improvement. It could carry information without a call. It could not supply the missing agreement to change another customer’s promise. Calling this a failure of AI would be as imprecise as crediting AI for the shared record: the fault was in the authority Northline had left undesigned.

Replace the decision, too

Sunder and Shaun, who looked after customers, worked through the two requests after the recovery. The existing reservation record had done its job; what was missing was a decision about changing a promise already made, and the authority to make that change had to include the consent of the customer whose agreed window would move, whose agreement could not be read from a capacity figure on a shared screen.

They kept the reservation rule and added a route for exceptions. Shaun would establish the customer consequence and whether an alternative was acceptable. Sunder could authorise the change within agreed service priorities only when the replacement arrangements were supported. Until then, the urgent customer would receive a clear answer: Northline had not accepted the request. A case outside those priorities went to Peter while there was still time for the decision to matter.

The arrangement preserved a route for judgment without restoring every daily conversation. Routine work could proceed with the shared information. A specific conflict would bring the relevant people together with a decision to make.

Sunder also stopped attending a recurring meeting that reviewed information already present in the operating record. The trial had shown no decision that depended on his presence there. Peter accepted the removal.

Both changes belonged to the same principle. Keep the function that earns its cost. Change or remove the activity that does not.

At Northline, one longstanding sign-off required Peter's approval for minor changes that already fitted an agreed service arrangement. He usually accepted them. When he was unavailable, they waited.

Thomas showed him several examples. No new trade-off had required Peter's authority. The team had already established the relevant conditions. Peter was being informed through a process that pretended to need a decision.

They replaced the approval with a visible record and a clear limit on what the team could change. Peter could inspect the changes. He no longer had to delay them to know they had happened.

If you are the kind of leader who likes to be close to the work, this distinction may be the one that costs you something: you have to find a way to know what is happening without making everyone wait for you. Access to information does not always require control over permission. If an approval exists mainly to reassure you that you remain involved, then the organisation is paying for your reassurance in other people's waiting time, and it is worth asking, before the next one goes on the list, whether you would buy that reassurance at that price if the invoice came to you.

A wider span has a price

Peter's interest in reducing routine coordination was legitimate. Northline could serve more work without adding a manager every time volume increased. Better information and delegated decisions might allow Sunder to cover a broader operating area.

Before assigning that span, they needed to estimate the remaining exception load. A manager can handle many routine cases when the rules and resources are clear. A smaller number of conflicting commitments can consume the same day.

Count the work that reaches the person after automation, including its variability. Ask what happens when several difficult cases arrive together. If routine tasks disappear but competing commitments, difficult assessments and urgent exceptions still reach the same desk, expanding the manager's span can spend the apparent saving before anyone has allowed time for the work that remains. Identify which decisions can be made elsewhere.

Sunder wanted relief from preventable interruptions. He did not want to become the emergency destination for a larger area whose ordinary systems concealed unresolved conflicts. Those were compatible preferences.

The company tested the revised decision route before expanding his remit. It watched whether conflicts reached him early enough, whether the authority matched the choices required and whether he could still examine recurring problems rather than only recover from them.

Effort can teach. It can also exhaust, exclude and conceal poor design. A difficult process is not educational merely because experienced people learned to survive it.

If removing a task would remove valuable practice, the organisation should identify the capability it needs and arrange a deliberate way to develop it. Making people repeat avoidable clerical work is an uncertain substitute for teaching. It may mostly teach them that improvement threatens somebody else's account of professionalism.

A company can remove a layer and become better at noticing trouble if the new system exposes useful patterns and sends real decisions to people who can act; it can also become more certain about its reports while the unresolved work travels through private messages nobody has time to read.

For this experiment, Peter kept Sunder’s remit unchanged until conflicts arrived early enough to settle. A faster information flow justified trying a different arrangement. It had not yet justified giving him more territory.

Sunder removed the obsolete meeting from his calendar. He left the exception decision route beside the dispatch screen, where a request to move a promise would have to find him before it became a promise to somebody else.

Section III · The Work

Context, authority, and tests in real work

8. Context, and the Unwritten Why-Not

The address had a note beside it: no access.

Northline's booking system treated that as a reason to reject a collection. The customer, who had received deliveries there for years, considered the answer absurd. Shaun took the call and asked dispatch what the note meant.

Sunder remembered the original problem. A larger vehicle had been unable to use the entrance specified in an old booking. The site had another entrance, and a smaller vehicle could make the collection. The note had preserved the refusal while losing the conditions that justified it.

Thomas, who built Northline's systems, had supplied the note to an assistant preparing booking decisions. The assistant had used relevant company information and reached an unhelpful conclusion. More access to the same note would not have improved the answer.

A rule is a compressed experience

An organisation accumulates decisions in fragments. Do not collect there. Speak to this person first. Leave extra time for that customer. Never change this field after confirmation.

Some of those fragments contain hard-won knowledge and some contain a workaround somebody meant to remove, a preference nobody else shared, or a conclusion that was reasonable under conditions that ended years ago, and the people who lived through the original event may know which is which, while a newcomer, or a system, reading the same record may have no reliable way to tell them apart.

AI assistance makes this problem newly consequential because it can turn stored information into proposals and actions quickly. A note that once prompted a colleague to ask Sunder may now be interpreted as sufficient authority to refuse a customer. An old exception can travel further than the person who remembers its origin, outlasting the vehicle it was written for, the manager who approved it and the customer whose entrance it described, until it is applied one morning to a case it was never meant to touch by someone who has no way of knowing that.

Useful context preserves enough of the reason to distinguish cases. The note should tell the next person which entrance and vehicle condition mattered, where the information came from and what would make the restriction worth checking again, so they can recognise a changed circumstance before repeating the refusal. That gives the next decision-maker something more useful than an instruction to obey or an invitation to improvise.

Thomas and Sunder replaced the broad refusal with this note:

The previous refusal concerned the front entrance with the larger vehicle. Sunder checked an alternative entrance suitable for the smaller vehicle. Ask the customer to confirm that entrance is available for this collection; dispatch must confirm the vehicle. Recheck if the entrance, vehicle or customer's instructions change.

From a message to a permitted action

The next request read: “Same place as last time, Thursday if you can, but use the side gate. Two cartons. Please tell me before I finish this job.” A conventional form could collect the same details if the customer entered them correctly. A service employee could read the message, find the account and ask the missing questions. Northline's previous process depended on that employee for almost every variation in wording.

Thomas set up a narrower role for the model. It proposed the customer, site, cartons and requested day from the message, leaving the collection window unresolved. Ordinary software looked up the matching account and retrieved the access note; the model used that note to draft the next question. A staff member could see both the source message and the proposed interpretation.

Part of the arrangement What it did
Model Interpreted varied wording and proposed a question or booking details.
Ordinary software Retrieved the site record, checked required fields and permissions, and recorded accepted changes.
Northline's decision Limited the model to proposals; required customer confirmation of access and dispatch confirmation of vehicle capacity before commitment.

The first proposed reply said the side gate was suitable. That was a plausible reading of “alternative entrance”, but the source note did not identify the customer's side gate as that entrance. Shaun caught the gap because the proposed reply appeared beside the note. He asked the customer to identify the entrance and sent the vehicle question to dispatch. Thomas retained the ambiguous-gate request among the cases used to check later changes to the workflow.

The model was contributing interpretation across untidy language. The lookup and permission checks were ordinary software. The requirement to reserve capacity before promising it was an operating decision Northline had already needed to make. Cheaper interpretation could reduce how often someone rebuilt a request by hand; it could not turn a suggestive match into established access.

The system also had to check the current booking when a change was finally accepted. A proposal prepared before another employee changed that booking could no longer be applied as though nothing had happened. The software stopped the conflicting update for reconsideration. Fluency supplied no reason to overwrite a newer commitment.

More information can make a worse account

A common response to missing context is to collect everything. A message records the first agreement, a transcript preserves an objection and an old decision states a rule that was later changed; putting all three within reach can reveal the history while leaving the system unable to tell which account governs the work. Retrieval has made the disagreement available. It has not settled it.

Thomas tried including the whole set of notes for a customer. One said the site closed at four; another said five. The system selected five from the newer note. When he checked the source, that time belonged to an exceptional Friday. A third message concerned another site under the same account name. More material had produced a confident answer to the wrong question.

A useful information system needs ways to identify source, scope and authority. It should make uncertainty visible when records disagree. The person using it should not have to assume that the most confidently worded or most recently retrieved sentence governs the work.

A model can help identify contradictions and propose a cleaner account. Somebody still needs to establish the relevant facts and decide which record should control a consequential action. Over time, more of that work may itself be assisted. The requirement remains that the resulting account has a basis the organisation can inspect.

Context has owners and costs

Sunder initially welcomed the idea of capturing the unwritten reasons. Then he looked at the list Thomas wanted him to review.

“When is this supposed to happen?”

The question was reasonable. The organisation had benefited from knowledge carried in his working day. Making it available in another form required additional work. If Northline wanted that work done, it had to allocate time and decide which parts mattered first.

Peter authorised a limited block for recurring exceptions affecting the workshop trial. The team would not attempt to document every possibility before proceeding. They chose cases likely to recur or to cause a consequential mistake. Other gaps would be recorded when encountered and assessed for later attention.

Without that arrangement a context project can become an extraction exercise, in which the knowledgeable person is asked to empty years of judgment into a system while continuing to do the job that generated the judgment in the first place, with no time set aside for either explaining what they know or keeping the account useful. Months later, stale information produces a failure and they are blamed for not maintaining what nobody gave them time to maintain.

Not every memory should travel

The fact that information could help a decision does not automatically justify making it widely available.

Think of a customer who mentions a private reason while rebooking, an employee who tells a manager privately why a shift is difficult, or an old note that calls someone unreliable without recording what happened or whether it was ever put right. Each detail may have helped one decision. That does not give it a place in every decision from now on, and carrying the record forward can carry the mistake, and sometimes the unfairness, with it.

Record what the work needs at the level at which it needs it. A scheduling constraint may be sufficient without the personal story behind it. A disputed assessment needs a route for challenge, not automatic promotion into an authoritative fact.

Access should follow a legitimate purpose and the obligations attached to the information. The exact duties vary with the setting; the operating principle is clear enough to begin with. Do not use the convenience of a shared system as a reason to erase boundaries that protected people in the original interaction.

Keep the reason open to revision

Later, the customer at the disputed address reported that the entrance arrangement had changed. Northline's improved note made the next step clearer: dispatch should verify the new access conditions and update the restriction if warranted.

The record did not have to be discarded because the world had changed; it had been written, this time, to say under what circumstances it should be reconsidered, which is the difference between a note that ages into a rule and a note that ages into a question.

At Northline, an address that had become a blanket refusal returned to the set of collections the business could consider. The customer did not see a more intelligent note. She received a useful question instead of a refusal.

9. Asking, Delegating, Stopping

The customer wanted Peter.

Sunder had refused a late change to an ordinary collection at Northline. He had checked the remaining capacity, examined the alternatives and concluded that accepting the request would put another confirmed commitment at risk. The rules Peter had approved gave him authority to stop that category of change.

The customer knew Peter and wanted to try a different route to the answer. Peter liked being able to solve a problem the process could not. Before returning the call, he looked at the authority he had actually given Sunder.

Before the customer called

That authority had been worked out while Thomas built an assisted rescheduling process. A customer had asked to move a collection to a second site while Shaun was on another call. The distance was modest; the new address was outside that customer’s approved locations.

The difference between a suggestion and an act

You can ask an assistant to consider a change without authorising the change. You can authorise a change without authorising every action that might help achieve it. Those distinctions are easy to lose when the same conversational interface appears to handle all three.

A request to find a better collection time is not yet permission to cancel the old booking, promise a new one or contact another party. Each action can change somebody else's options. The customer may arrange staff around the new time. Dispatch may allocate capacity that another customer then cannot obtain. Reversing a digital record will not necessarily reverse those consequences.

Delegation begins with a result and the authority required to pursue it. The result must be observable, and the limits must be usable while the work is happening: before a booking changes, a charge is waived or another person arranges their afternoon around an offer you did not mean to authorise.

At Northline, the initial service could change a booking among already approved alternatives when capacity was available and the customer's terms remained unchanged. It could not create a new service arrangement, waive a charge or cancel the only confirmed collection while searching for another. Those decisions required a person with the appropriate authority.

The boundaries made useful autonomy possible. Without them, Northline faced an unhelpful choice between letting every request become an unrestricted commitment and having a person inspect everything. With them, ordinary cases could move quickly while exceptional cases received attention for a specific reason.

This is the commercial promise of better delegation: customers obtain a useful answer while it still matters, and people spend less time acting as a communications channel between systems that already contain enough information.

The stop that went nowhere

Thomas began with the ordinary flow because it was easier to build. The request arrived, the system checked the conditions, the change was recorded and the customer received confirmation. The demonstration was satisfying because every participant in it behaved as expected, which is the ordinary condition of demonstrations and the reason Sunder, who had spent his working life watching participants not behave as expected, asked to see the case that would stop.

Thomas entered the second-site request. The process identified the boundary and marked it for review. The original booking remained intact. That was better than accidentally replacing it, but the request now sat in a list nobody routinely watched during dispatch's busy period.

They assigned the handover to the service role covering booking changes, with dispatch available for the operating decision. The test record now read:

Existing collection: first site, confirmed. Requested change: second site, not approved for this customer's arrangement. No booking altered. Service cover must obtain dispatch's decision before the afternoon route is released; if no answer is possible, contact the customer before that point. Customer told: your first-site booking remains confirmed while we examine the change.

Sunder read it and pointed to the route-release condition. That was the last useful decision point, not an arbitrary response target. The assigned service cover acknowledged the case; it no longer disappeared into an unattended review list.

Shaun could then handle the question without reconstructing it from several records. He would not promise the alternative until someone had accepted its operational consequences. If it could not be decided in time, the customer would receive that answer while another choice remained possible.

The arrangement used human attention selectively. It did not treat attention as infinitely available. Covering the handover was part of a paid role, and somebody had to own it when the usual person was absent. A sentence saying “escalate to a human” would have left those decisions unmade.

A tempting inference is that adding a human approval makes a system safer. Sometimes it does: the person has relevant knowledge and can examine a few consequential cases. But a thousand approvals assigned to an already occupied person can be less honest than a narrow automated permission that is actually enforced. The question is how much scrutiny the arrangement can supply when several difficult cases arrive together.

Beyond Northline

The stopped booking had a customer on the other side of it. Inside the depot we can watch the list acquire an owner; outside it, the person waiting may see only that their request is being reviewed.

Put yourself beside a housing applicant whose tenancy decision is pending, a borrower querying a refusal or a parent waiting for a school placement: the record can remain safely unchanged while another deadline passes, another option closes and the cost of waiting falls on someone the review queue does not count.

I want the word escalated to describe a handover somebody has accepted. It should also tell the person waiting what remains in force and when they will receive an answer, including an answer that the review is incomplete.

When you next design a stop rule, ask what the case does while it waits, and who is waiting with it.

What the model contributes

Consider the incoming message: “We have moved the crates to the other site; can you pick up there instead?” A fixed form could collect a new address reliably if the customer used it. The model offers a different convenience: it can interpret this varied language and propose the relevant amendment without asking the customer to reconstruct the request in Northline’s categories.

Ordinary software then looks up the booking, checks whether the proposed location is permitted, and refuses to overwrite a record that has changed since it was read. It records whether a change was completed. The model’s confidence cannot create permission or reserve capacity that has already gone.

In the test, the proposal was intelligible and the address check worked. The failure was the unattended review list. Thomas had to repair the handover, not improve the wording of the model's refusal, because the refusal had been perfectly clear and had gone to a list nobody read, and no amount of clarity survives arriving where no one is looking. Peter had to allocate cover and decide which ordinary amendments could complete without it.

Give discretion where the evidence supports it

Peter wanted a faster service and was willing to accept that ordinary changes should no longer pass through him. He asked Thomas and Sunder to establish the first set of cases that could proceed under the rule.

They chose a limited class with known information and a usable record of completion. They tested those cases, including interrupted updates and competing requests for the same remaining capacity. They also examined whether the system could detect when required information was absent. A process that reliably performs a permitted action still needs to recognise when permission has not been established.

Once that work was complete, Peter authorised the bounded operation. Customers making qualifying changes received an answer without waiting for Shaun to finish another call. The benefit was visible in a completed transaction, not a claim about the number of messages generated.

Peter did not need to inspect every success to remain responsible for the arrangement. He needed a basis for the initial authority, a way to observe whether it continued to fit and a means of changing it. Thomas retained records that allowed a problematic change to be traced. Sunder could suspend the affected category if the operating assumptions ceased to hold. Broadening the scope required another explicit decision.

Delegation should be able to expand when evidence warrants it and contract when conditions change, so that an early precaution does not become a permanent restriction on useful work and an old success does not become permanent permission to act. Pride in being automated cannot supply the missing evidence.

The second-site request did not receive the instant approval the customer wanted. Shaun reached the customer after dispatch examined the alternative. Northline could make the change under a separately agreed arrangement, or retain the original booking. The customer chose the alternative with its terms made clear.

Back to Peter’s call

Before returning the call, he asked Sunder for the facts. There was no overlooked ordinary option. Making this collection would require revising another promise or buying an exceptional arrangement at a cost the account would not support. Peter could change the commercial decision if he chose to spend the money, but he could not honestly describe that as a correction to Sunder's judgment, because Sunder had judged correctly, and what Peter would be buying was a different answer at a price the account did not support, with a possible cost to Sunder's authority that would not appear on any account at all.

Peter returned the call and explained the available alternatives. The customer could retain the confirmed collection or purchase an exceptional arrangement on separately agreed terms. Northline could not provide the requested change within the existing price and commitments.

The customer moved that job to another carrier. Peter did not know whether the decision would affect future work. Sunder's stop had a real commercial cost, which was precisely why the support meant something.

Backing a person does not settle the facts

A manager can turn protection into another kind of evasion. Loyalty to the team becomes a reason to dismiss customer evidence or avoid examining an error. That arrangement may feel safe internally while making the business difficult to rely on.

Peter checked the facts before backing the decision. If Sunder had misunderstood capacity or applied the wrong terms, the answer should have changed. The team would then need to understand the correction. A mistaken judgment within legitimate authority should not require a humiliating performance, but neither should it become untouchable.

The distinction is between protecting a person's right to decide within the arrangement and declaring every decision they make correct, and good management holds the first while staying able to examine the second, which is harder than it sounds, because the person whose decision is being examined may hear the examination as a withdrawal of the protection.

When you reverse someone, say why in a form they could repeat to a colleague: if new information changed the answer, name the information; if you are making a commercial exception, call it one and say what it costs, so that the person who followed the rule is not made to look incompetent for declining to spend money they were not authorised to spend.

Suppose Peter had decided that retaining the customer's account justified buying exceptional capacity. He could have said that Sunder's operational judgment stood, and that he was authorising an additional commercial expense. The team would then know what changed. Without that explanation, the lesson would be that enough pressure can make an unavailable vehicle appear.

People learn how authority works from these moments. The lesson travels further than a training session about empowerment because it concerns what happens when a decision has a price.

A technical answer may now be available to anyone in the team. The boss still controls whether a sound answer is permitted to cost the business something. That is why removing the boss from routine approval does not remove the need for leadership.

Peter recorded the lost job. He did not ask Sunder to recover the revenue through a riskier booking, and he left the limit in force. If similar requests accumulated, they would examine a separately priced service. For this afternoon, the customer had gone elsewhere.

10. Touching the Real Thing

Consider a hypothetical pilot. A translation agency tests an assisted overnight service. Every document arrives on time, clients praise the work, and the pilot loses money. The senior editor reviewed every page; the next ten prospective clients work in a specialist field the editor rarely handles.

Would you accept them, stop the service or buy another test? Choose an action, the fact it depends on and the cost you are willing to bear. Keep that choice beside Northline's result.

Northline’s collections happened. That was the awkward part of the review.

Northline had completed a limited trial for twelve workshops. The booking process worked. Customers understood the collection arrangement. The goods entered Northline's existing service. A few requests needed intervention, but the team handled them within the trial's stated terms.

Peter had watched one collection himself. The workshop owner could finish another job because she knew when Northline would arrive. This was the usefulness he had hoped to create.

Then Ava set out the cost of providing it.

The workshops were dispersed. Before the trial, Sunder had expected to fit their collections into spare intervals on existing routes. In the live operation, those intervals did not line up with the workshops' windows and the onward service's departure times. Northline had needed a separate block of vehicle-and-driver time to honour the collections. A service could be appreciated, competently delivered and commercially unsuitable in its present form.

Peter wanted to try more customers.

“More where?” Ava asked.

Test the promise you intend to sell

Northline's earlier demonstrations had shown useful quotation assistance, clearer booking language and bounded rescheduling. Those gains remained valuable. The workshop trial asked a further question: could the company deliver a recurring collection offer at a cost the offer could support?

The twelve workshops were the customers ready to commit before the association's deadline. Northline had looked for a compact group but had not secured one. Sunder's proposal gave the dispersed trial a different commercial hypothesis: the freight could share journeys the firm was already making. The team knew a dedicated collection block would defeat the offer at this price. The trial budget covered the cost of discovering whether that block could be avoided.

The distinction was worth testing because a route's apparent spare time was only an estimate until the extra collections met its ordinary obligations. Customer availability had been checked; compatibility with the whole working day had not.

The trial covered two collections for each of twelve paying workshops: one in week four and one in week five of Northline's six-week investigation. Its terms were limited. One scheduled collection per workshop per week included up to two ordinary cartons within specified handling limits, carried through the existing regional service. Urgent bespoke work was outside the offer. Customers knew the trial did not guarantee a continuing service at that price.

The dollar amounts in this example are teaching assumptions for this service, not logistics prices or estimates of a real firm's costs.

Weekly account at the trial volume Amount ($)
Twelve workshops paying $120 each 1,440
Assigned collection transport block 1,650
Incremental handling and onward carriage 240
Paid booking and support time 210
Expected recovery allowance 180
Defined weekly service cost 2,280
Contribution before wider costs −840

The transport block includes assigned vehicle and driver time and operating expenses. The account excludes development and wider company overhead. Recovery is an allowance to compare with actual incidents, not an assertion that exactly that amount was spent every week. These definitions matter because a tidy total can conceal a different business from the one being considered.

At this volume and arrangement, the weekly service account was $840 short before the wider costs. Northline could fund a bounded experiment from its agreed pilot budget. It could not describe the shortfall as an established business merely because the software had performed well.

Look at the loss closely enough to learn

Peter initially treated the twelve customers as evidence that the service needed scale. More revenue could indeed help if it fitted the same transport and support capacity, but if each new customer brought another long detour or an incompatible window, growth would not dilute the problem so much as reproduce it at a larger scale, with more vehicles committed to the same mistake and more customers waiting on the same unexamined assumption. Customer count alone could not settle the question.

Ava's account separated the costs so the team could inspect that distinction. Administration was no longer the only expensive part. Geography and the terms customers would accept now deserved more attention.

Sunder put the working route beside Peter's proposed additions. One workshop's goods became available just as the nearby vehicle had to leave for an existing delivery. Collecting on its return would miss the onward departure. The vehicle passed close to the customer; that did not make the customer's work fit the journey.

“There is space in it,” Peter said.

“There is,” Sunder replied. “There isn't another morning.”

Dennis had noticed how little of the load space some legs used. More freight could improve that figure while requiring another journey. The live trial had exposed a time constraint that a map of nearby vehicles concealed.

Count the work that rescued the result

A pilot often receives attention unavailable to ordinary operations. The founder calls a customer, a specialist watches every transaction and a colleague stays late to repair something quietly; together they deliver a useful result that the proposed service may never reproduce at the price and staffing recorded in the trial. Keep their contribution in the account.

At Northline, paid booking and support time remained visible. The team recorded interventions and the reason for them. If Peter handled a call, they did not infer that the call would cost nothing in a continuing service. Somebody would have to own that work when he was elsewhere.

Be particularly careful when a customer reports satisfaction. They may be rating the exceptional team's whole service, including the founder's call, the specialist's attention and the repair nobody charged for, while your forecast assumes a much smaller team can produce the same experience repeatedly. Their satisfaction is real. Its cost remains part of the decision.

Give the deadline an answer

The workshop association had asked for Northline's answer within six weeks because it was considering a rival's fixed-day offer. The deadline did not disappear when Northline discovered a more complicated question.

In the sixth week, Peter and Shaun gave the answer they could support. Northline would complete its trial obligations, but would not continue or expand the dispersed offer at the trial price. Existing ordinary services remained available on their own terms. The company wanted permission to discuss a different arrangement later; the association should make its current plans without relying on that possibility.

Some members chose the rival. Shaun disliked losing business to a competitor whose actual delivery he could not assess. He also knew that asking customers to wait would make them finance Northline's unresolved design through uncertainty.

Peter did not call the outcome a successful launch. He called it a completed test that had prevented a larger commitment and identified a question worth pursuing. The team had created a useful service for the trial period. It had learned that this version should stop.

What would the next test buy?

The translation pilot poses the same question through different work. More clients could improve the account if the editor's attention had spare capacity; unfamiliar subject matter could instead require another costly layer of review. A sound next test would measure the recurring effort for the work the agency actually intended to accept. Stopping could also be justified if the available price plainly could not support it. Praise cannot choose between those actions, because someone can welcome an idea without having to pay its price or bear the work of using it; the next encounter needs to test the fact that remains unresolved, with enough at stake for the answer to guide a real commitment. Payment tests something an enthusiastic interview cannot. Live delivery tests something a screen cannot. In Northline's case, no number of simulated bookings could establish whether a driver would reach a dispersed workshop before its goods, its opening hours and the onward departure ceased to fit together.

Northline ended the trial with working software, customers it had served, a costly service pattern it would not repeat unchanged and a better question. Peter kept the workshop owner's account of what dependable collection had allowed her to do. Ava kept the cost account beside it.

The opportunity had to answer to both.

Section IV · The People

Work, transitions, and the formation of judgment

11. Two Speeds

Dennis learned about the new handling target when somebody asked why he was below it.

He worked on the floor at Northline. The target appeared in an operating summary alongside other measures of the depot's work. It had been prepared with assistance from a system Dennis had not used and from an account of the work he had not been asked to examine.

He had used AI for something else. A few weeks earlier, he had organised examples of unclear labels into a proposal the team could discuss. He liked the fact that he could make a practical point without waiting for someone to translate it into a presentation.

Now the technology reached him from the other direction.

Thomas, Northline's systems builder, had spent paid time trying tools, rejecting unsuitable outputs and changing his approach. Dennis was being asked to explain a result generated through a process he could not yet inspect. Both men worked in a company adopting AI. That description concealed the important difference between their situations.

Permission and exposure

One speed of change is the speed at which a person can experiment. The other is the speed at which decisions shaped by the technology reach them.

An employee may have little opportunity to try a tool while already being scheduled, evaluated or served through systems that use it; the manager introducing the programme may experience it mainly as additional options, while the employee experiences a revised obligation. These speeds need not match.

A tempting inference is that widening access widens agency: put the same capability in everyone's hands and people gain a practical means to shape their work. Dennis's label proposal was a reason to believe it. He could now express a useful objection without waiting for a manager to translate it.

The inference fails when access is asked to stand for control over a different decision. Thomas could discard an unhelpful draft before it affected anybody. Dennis could not discard a performance target. Equal software access would leave that difference intact. Where someone controls the task, can decline the output and has time to learn, access may supply most of the missing agency. Where an institution uses an output to allocate work or pay, the person also needs a usable way to contest its authority.

Peter, who ran Northline, initially wanted to address the concern through training. He had seen Dennis's label proposal and wanted more people to discover similar uses. He proposed a short session after the depot's main work was finished.

Dennis asked whether attendance would be paid. Another employee asked what would happen to the remaining work if the session took place during a shift. The questions brought the proposal out of the language of opportunity and into the actual day.

Make participation possible

Peter moved the sessions into paid working time and arranged cover. They used actual tasks people wanted help with: explaining a recurring problem, comparing instructions and preparing a question for another team. Nobody needed to pretend every example was useful.

The aim was not to make the depot reproduce Thomas's working style, which would have mistaken his use of the assistance for everyone else's need, but to let each person find a task in their own week that the assistance made lighter, and to notice, without being told, the ones it made heavier. Some people wanted assistance with writing. Others wanted to understand what the systems involved in their work could and could not do. A useful session allowed those aims to coexist.

Thomas discovered that his demonstration was hard to follow beside shared equipment. He went back to the previous screen and apologised. Someone asked him to go back one more. Dennis pulled over a chair for the next person; standing had made the whole thing feel like waiting for a machine to be repaired. They began again, using examples from their own shifts. One instruction became clearer. Another suggestion lost an important condition, which the employee put back.

Training does not settle the assessment

After the session, Dennis returned to the target.

“I can use the tool,” he told Peter. “That doesn't tell me why it says I should be doing this much.”

Peter asked for the basis of the target: what work it counted, what differences it allowed for and how someone could challenge an unsuitable comparison. The assessment would receive a separate examination. Dennis's question was recorded rather than absorbed into a discussion of his attitude toward technology.

The full answer would take work. Northline had recently changed some of its customer mix, and the handling measure might not represent the resulting difference in loads.

Sunder asked whether the disputed flag should still count when assigning paid relief responsibility. Peter said to keep the existing assessment process until the review produced an answer. Changing the yardstick halfway through seemed unfair to the other employees.

That decision kept one kind of consistency by exposing Dennis to a comparison Peter could not yet defend. Recording a concern had not suspended its consequences.

The cost of a recoverable mistake

When people experiment, ask what happens if the attempt fails.

A senior leader may lose an hour and retain discretion, a junior employee may be judged careless for an equivalent error, and a contractor may fear losing the next assignment, so that a common permission to experiment creates very different practical invitations. The policy can be broad while the room to try remains narrow.

Create a bounded setting in which a poor result can be examined without becoming a general judgment on the person. Specify what information may be used, which outputs require checking and what remains an experiment. Give the person a realistic way to obtain help.

Peter told the depot team which exercises remained internal and who could help check a proposed change. He did not promise that any use of a tool would be approved. He made a specific part of the work available for learning without asking employees to gamble on an undefined reaction.

Beyond Northline

Dennis is inside the building. He can find Peter and ask why the target applies to him. Even that proximity has not prevented a loss. The scene cannot show what it takes to challenge a decision when you do not know who made it.

This is more than an imagined extension of the depot. In 2023, the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission announced a settlement with iTutorGroup after alleging that its application software automatically rejected older applicants because of their age.[1] The case concerns automated screening; it is not evidence about a conversational model or a measure of how often such discrimination occurs. It establishes that the person affected need not be the person using the system.

An applicant can prepare carefully, submit the information requested, receive an apparently final answer and have no opportunity to present the fact that would change it, while the people operating the service describe their improvement in terms of how many applications it now processes. Both accounts can describe the same operation. Only one includes the lost chance.

The applicant may be you. You can lead a team with considerable discretion during the day and encounter another institution as a record in the evening. Familiarity with AI gives you no automatic access to the evidence behind that institution's decision.

I do not assume every automated refusal is wrong or every human decision fair. I want the account of adoption to include the people whose options the system changes. Count them alongside the users. Then examine a real route of challenge: whether someone can discover what needs correcting, reach a person with relevant authority and obtain reconsideration before the opportunity disappears.

Some decisions properly remain refusals. Some are governed by obligations you cannot alter. Those limits need an intelligible account too. Ask whether the route you offer is one you could actually use if you had only the information, time and standing of the person receiving the decision.

Dennis left the session with another use he wanted to try. On the next relief list, his name was absent.

Note

[1] US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, iTutorGroup to Pay $365,000 to Settle EEOC Discriminatory Hiring Suit, 11 September 2023. Settlement of allegations concerning age-based automated application screening; not a finding about generative AI or the prevalence of automated discrimination.

12. What Happens to a Trade

Fewer routine calls can produce a harder working day. Northline's quieter service queue was beginning to demonstrate why.

Shaun's team had stopped entering the same details twice. Some ordinary amendments now went through within agreed limits without anyone touching them. The hours that used to go on relaying straightforward information between a caller and dispatch were coming back, and the question was which work needed them now.

The failed workshop collection trial had not produced this gain. Those improvements were working in Northline's existing service, where customers continued booking and changing shipments every day, which meant the gain was real and measurable, even though it established nothing about whether the new business Peter hoped to build would pay its way.

When a routine service-administration position became vacant, Peter wanted to examine the work before replacing it. Shaun, who looked after customers, agreed that the old job description no longer described the whole need.

He also knew what was left in the calls that reached his team. They contained more disagreement, missing information and exceptions. A quieter queue did not necessarily make an easier day.

The task, the job and the market

Shaun's team spent less time confirming bookings and more time resolving awkward requests. Its tasks had changed. Whether Northline needed the same post, hours and pay was a question about the job, which Peter's vacancy review had yet to settle. What customer-service skill would earn across the region was a third question, about the trade. Customers, other employers and people entering the work would help determine that. Northline's quieter queue could not answer for them.

I become suspicious when a presentation calls the remaining work “higher value.” Sometimes it is: people gain room to use skills they wanted to exercise, with authority to resolve the case and time to think. But the label tells me none of that.

Shaun's quieter queue exposed the other possibility. A routine confirmation had once separated one difficult call from another. Now a customer disputing a missed promise was followed by a customer asking for something dispatch could not provide, then by a third whose explanation was incomplete. The easy calls had supplied changes of pace and cases through which a newcomer learned what normal work looked like. Removing them improved one account of the day.

I would be persuaded by a fuller account: greater discretion, protected recovery time, fewer unresolved cases, better pay, or employees saying the work had improved and being free to say otherwise. A harder job deserves more than a flattering description.

Until then, I want “higher value” followed by a name. More valuable to whom?

Lower cost can expand demand and reduce labour together

Northline's ordinary bookings took less effort. If a cheaper service attracted more customers or more frequent shipments, the company could grow while needing fewer hours per booking. Peter needed evidence about both movements before estimating the work left for his team.

Total employment depends on the relationship between demand and labour per unit, along with other changes: customers may buy more of the cheaper service while each purchase requires less work, and those two movements can pull the staffing decision in opposite directions. Neither alone tells you the final number of jobs.

Northline had evidence for reduced routine effort in its own operation. It did not yet have evidence that a new customer segment would support enough profitable demand to absorb all the released capacity. The workshop trial had shown precisely why that second claim needed its own test.

Peter therefore separated the vacancy decision from a promise about future growth. He could say that the old bundle of tasks no longer justified automatic replacement, and he could say it to Shaun's face with the evidence beside him. What he could not say, because nothing at Northline had established it, was that everyone would gain in the end because the technology would eventually create opportunities, a reassurance easy to offer before anyone has tested the opportunity on which it depends.

The people who adjust are not always the people who lost

When US cities mechanised telephone switching, women already working as operators faced a different future from the young women who came after them. Researchers found that other work offset the lost entry occupation for those later groups. The women already doing the job were more likely subsequently to be in lower-paying work or outside employment.[1] The local labour market could adjust while the people whose work had disappeared still lost ground.

The example does not predict AI's employment effects. It exposes a distinction that matters whenever someone says the economy adjusted. Which people adjusted, over what period, and on what terms?

A leader has a particular responsibility to avoid borrowing an aggregate possibility as a promise to an individual. New roles elsewhere do not establish that an employee can obtain them. A new task inside the company does not establish that the employee can learn it in the available time or accept its hours.

Equally, protecting every existing task indefinitely can make the business less capable of supporting anyone. The obligation is to make the actual choices visible and improve the attainable transitions. It is not to deny change until the organisation loses the means to respond.

Beyond Northline

Northline's vacancy makes the choice visible inside one employer. It cannot tell you what leaving that employer would mean. The telephone-switching research concerns the United States in 1920–1940, not a universal sequence through which every labour market must pass.

If you lead a team in a market with low wages, intermittent connectivity, informal employment or little affordable retraining, the cost of buying and maintaining an automated service may compare very differently with the work it replaces, and the person asked to move may have fewer usable alternatives. Elsewhere, negotiated transition terms or funded training may change both the employer's costs and the employee's choices.

Read the next two chapters with those differences beside you. Price the actual task, find out which protections apply and ask what work someone could obtain locally on terms they could accept. An occupational forecast cannot supply those answers. Test these three chapters against your market, including the people its official job descriptions leave out.

Bring the market back to the vacancy

At Northline, Peter asked Shaun to describe the emerging work before agreeing a replacement role. They identified routine tasks that had reduced, exceptions that required more attention and the times customers needed access to someone with authority. They also identified what the team should no longer be expected to solve through personal improvisation, a category that can go unwritten because the improvising is invisible while it works and only becomes visible on the day the person who did it is not there.

Examine bargaining power separately from competence

A person can become better at their work while the price paid for it falls. If many others gain access to the same assistance, improved output may become the expected baseline. The person may produce more without retaining much of the benefit.

Conversely, someone who can resolve a problem others cannot readily handle may gain negotiating power without their visible output changing at all: Shaun can explain what a changed collection means to a customer, Sunder can judge what dispatch can actually carry, and Dennis can distinguish handling difficulties an ordinary summary may conceal. Whether any of that keeps its bargaining value depends on the market around them and the institutions inside it, not simply on how hard they worked to acquire it.

Moral worth, practical competence and market leverage are different things. A person can become more capable, discover that many others can now supply the same result and receive a lower price for it, without anything in that sequence establishing that their effort was wasted or their life is worth less. A relationship should not be reduced to a negotiation over scarcity.

The entry route is part of the trade

Routine work has often served as a way into a more demanding role. If that work shrinks, the organisation needs to ask where future competence will come from. A person cannot be hired already experienced forever if no one creates the experience.

A trade can change every tool and still keep a way in. It can also excel at today's work while failing to teach tomorrow's workers. Peter's replacement job description needed to explain how a newcomer would learn to handle difficult calls, as well as who would answer them today.

Write the role in the future tense carefully

Peter left the routine service-administration vacancy unfilled while Northline worked through the changing workday, its coverage needs and the terms of a replacement role. Existing employees remained employed on their current terms during the review. He did not treat a pause in recruitment as proof of a permanent cash saving that could fund an unrelated promise.

Shaun could see a useful future service role taking shape. He could also see that its coverage demands might not fit his own life. The trade was changing in a way he understood. What he would do about it was a separate decision.

Note

[1] James Feigenbaum and Daniel P. Gross, Answering the Call of Automation, NBER working paper 28061, revised February 2024. The study concerns US telephone switching adoption and labour-market adjustment in 1920–1940; the historical cohort distinction does not establish future AI employment outcomes.

13. Telling the Truth to People

Shaun read the proposed hours twice. He had understood them correctly the first time.

The revised service role at Northline needed coverage later in the day. Ordinary bookings and amendments now required less manual work, but the exceptions that reached a person still needed decisions while customers and dispatch could act on them. Peter wanted Northline to provide a more dependable response across that period.

Shaun understood the business reason. He had spent enough afternoons finding answers for customers to explain it himself. He could not sustainably provide the proposed coverage.

Peter had prepared a description of how customer service was changing. It was accurate and largely irrelevant to the question Shaun needed answered.

“Is that going to be my job?”

“The role needs to change.”

“I know. Are those the hours you're asking me to work?”

Separate the decision from the reassurance

A consequential conversation often becomes vague because several things have been mixed together. Some decisions are already made. Others remain open. The leader wants to preserve trust, avoid an unsupported assurance and explain the company's needs, and begins gathering those intentions into language so broad that the employee cannot tell which choice still belongs to them.

Peter could state that Northline needed later coverage for unresolved customer cases. He could state that the old service-administration vacancy would not be filled automatically in its previous form. He had not decided that Shaun alone must provide the coverage. Nor had the company established a funded alternative that guaranteed Shaun an unchanged role indefinitely.

Peter put the proposal aside and answered directly. The later coverage was a real requirement and Peter said so; assigning all of it to Shaun was still a proposal and Peter said that too, because the two sentences belonged together and separating them could make an unsettled choice about one person's life sound like a requirement the business had no power to change. Northline would examine a shared arrangement, but could not yet promise that it would work. Shaun's current terms would remain in place during a four-week funded review period.

Ava had confirmed the temporary provision. Northline would arrange paid cover for the gap while the review proceeded. Peter named who would develop the alternative and when they would return to Shaun with specific terms. The promise was limited, but it contained something Shaun could rely on.

Tell the truth about what consultation can change

Consultation has substance when a person's response can alter a choice that remains open. It becomes theatre when the organisation asks for views after deciding everything material.

At Northline, the need for coverage was supported by actual ordinary-service demand. The failed workshop trial was over and did not justify a continuing labour requirement. Peter could not invoke an exciting future service to make present hours appear inevitable.

How to provide coverage remained alterable. A shared role, a different allocation of work or a revised service promise might meet the need at different costs. Shaun could contribute to that design because he understood the work. He was also entitled to evaluate the proposal as a person whose own life would be affected.

“What can you do?” Peter asked.

Shaun gave the hours he could sustain. Peter began to ask why, then stopped. He already knew the constraint he had to design around.

“Could you cover the later part occasionally?”

“Occasionally becomes the arrangement when nobody else is there.”

Peter had intended a small flexibility. Shaun heard the part of the proposal most likely to grow. They wrote down that the shared arrangement would need actual later cover, including an alternative when that person was absent.

Uncertainty is already being carried

Leaders sometimes delay a difficult conversation because the outcome is uncertain. There can be sound reasons to avoid circulating undeveloped speculation. People should not be made to live under every possibility considered in a planning meeting.

But once a proposal has become consequential enough to shape staffing, work or expectations, silence is also an allocation of uncertainty. The organisation continues preparing while the person has less time to consider alternatives.

“I need the next date,” Shaun said. “I may need to look elsewhere.”

Peter looked up. He had hoped the review would keep Shaun engaged in Northline's future.

“Before we've worked this through?”

“While we work it through.”

Peter wrote down the date. The funded review bought Northline time to examine an alternative. It did not buy Shaun's agreement to wait for that answer before considering his own.

Do not make kindness depend on agreement

A difficult employment conversation can turn punitive without a raised voice: the leader's warmth is quietly withdrawn when the explanation is not accepted, the opportunity that was offered becomes evidence of ingratitude when it is declined, a request for time to think is read as resistance, and the person on the other side of the desk learns that the price of being treated well was agreement.

Peter needed to keep the funded review in place even if Shaun remained unhappy. He also needed to be honest about the limits. The company could investigate a shared arrangement; it could not create an indefinite role with no work it could afford to support. Respect required stating that limit without using it as a threat to end the discussion.

Shaun proposed retaining his existing pattern while another person took the later work. Peter agreed to cost and test the arrangement. He did not agree in advance that its additional handovers and expense were acceptable.

They now shared the relevant facts and still had different preferences. Shaun wanted a role compatible with his existing life. Peter wanted reliable coverage at a cost the service could sustain. A truthful conversation had made the disagreement clearer. It had not removed it.

Support is a commitment with an owner

An organisation can offer training, time to explore another role, help with a transition or a temporary arrangement. For the person planning around it, the offer needs a funded place, an available period and someone responsible for delivery, so that accepting support does not mean discovering its conditions one obstacle at a time.

Northline's immediate commitment was the paid four-week review under current terms, with temporary cover funded and a specific alternative examined. No future position was guaranteed. The review would produce an answer with actual hours, responsibilities and compensation, or an honest statement that no suitable arrangement had been found.

The legal and contractual obligations of a real employer would also govern its choices. The leadership point does not replace them. It concerns the quality of the account the person receives within those obligations, which is to say whether it is accurate, whether it arrives while there is still something they can do with it, and whether it is specific enough that they could take it to someone else and have that person understand what has been decided and what has not.

Peter sent Shaun a short written record after the conversation. It distinguished the coverage requirement, the open staffing design and the temporary commitment. Shaun corrected one sentence that made his participation sound like acceptance of the proposed role. Peter changed it.

The answer four weeks later

Ava put the costed arrangement on the table. Shaun could stay on a fixed earlier pattern at four-fifths of his previous hours and weekly pay, at the same compensation rate. The work had been reduced to fit: difficult customer cases and scheduled teaching, with no availability outside those hours. Nadia had volunteered for additional paid later coverage, with authority for its exceptions, and would become Maya's alternate supervisor.

Shaun ran his finger along the weekly-pay line.

“So the rate stays the same.”

“Yes,” Peter said.

“And I take home less.”

“Yes.”

Ava showed where the arrangement would be funded: the current service budget and unused recruitment provision, with another service improvement deferred to cover the remaining cost. She had not presented it as a saving for Northline. The company was paying to preserve useful experience and meet the later demand in a different way.

Shaun asked whether the deferred improvement could wait longer, leaving enough for more of his old hours. Peter did not want to make that longer commitment.

Shaun took out his phone and opened the calculator. He entered a number Peter could not see. They had spent most of the meeting discussing the shape of the role. Now Peter waited while Shaun considered something the role description did not contain.

After a while, Shaun locked the phone.

“I'll take it.”

Peter reached for the agreement.

“I still think you could have found the hours,” Shaun said.

Peter left the document where it was.

The temporary arrangement would end after a paid handover the following week. Nadia's later coverage would not give her an unlimited day either. If she was absent, the designated service cover had to take the case within its authority; the plan could not quietly grow a second version in which everybody called Shaun.

“Put the teaching in the actual week,” he said. “Not in the bit everyone thinks I've got left.”

Peter wrote it into the assignment.

14. The Apprentice Problem

Maya finished the routine requests faster than the team had expected.

She had recently joined Northline's service operation as a trainee. Northline had improved its booking systems, and an assistant could help interpret requests, find relevant information and prepare clear replies. Maya used it carefully enough to produce work that looked ready.

Then a customer asked Northline to collect a machine part. The request gave an ordinary address and a familiar weight. Further down, the customer wrote that the driver would need to remove it from the machine. The proposed reply offered a collection window. Maya checked the wording and was about to send it when Shaun stopped beside her desk.

“Who is taking it off the machine?”

“The driver, I think.”

“That's what the customer thinks too. Have we agreed to do that?”

She looked back at the request. Northline had been asked to perform work before there was a consignment ready to collect. Its ordinary collection terms did not include dismantling machinery. The reply was clear about a time and silent about the condition that made the time useful.

Shaun could show her the difference. The more difficult question was what Northline had arranged for her to learn it.

The old route into competence had included many ordinary cases, conversations and corrections. Some of that work had now become unnecessary. The company could not rely on experience accumulating in the same way while congratulating itself for removing the occasions that had supplied it.

Output is not the whole education

A business needs useful work now. It also needs people capable of doing consequential work later. The two requirements have often been financed through the same job.

A new employee performs simpler tasks, encounters variations and makes mistakes that an experienced colleague can correct before they become larger commitments, so that the same paid hours contribute to today's production and supply the comparisons from which tomorrow's judgment develops.

This arrangement has never been perfect. It can waste time, offer poor teaching and reserve good experience for favoured people. But when routine production is automated, whatever learning it provided does not automatically move into the remaining work.

The company may obtain faster output while the new employee has fewer opportunities to develop the distinctions needed for unusual cases. An assistant can make the result look competent before the user can explain why it fits. Equally, well-designed assistance can expose reasoning, provide feedback and give a beginner access to help previously unavailable.

In a study published in 2025, researchers examined the staggered deployment of an assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents. Less experienced workers made larger gains. The researchers also found evidence consistent with learning when assistance became unavailable during outages. That is a stronger result than faster assisted replies alone; it still does not establish mastery of every unfamiliar case or a general route into a profession.[1]

I want more people to be able to contribute, not merely more work to bear their names. That purpose requires asking what a beginner can now notice and decide, alongside what their assistant can produce. The two can improve together; they should be examined separately.

Define what the learner must become able to notice

Shaun began by listing the situations Maya needed to recognise before receiving broader authority. The list described decisions, not hours spent in training or numbers of replies sent.

Could she distinguish a requested collection from a confirmed one? Could she identify when the available information was insufficient? Could she recognise a condition outside the ordinary service terms and bring it to dispatch with the relevant facts? Could she explain to a customer what remained unresolved without accidentally making a promise?

For each of those, Maya needed examples that varied in the relevant way and not merely in volume, because a hundred routine cases can teach a person what routine looks like without preparing them for the afternoon when a request arrives wearing the appearance of routine and is not. Repeating an already explained case could show recall. A new case could show whether she recognised the distinction when its surface changed.

Shaun asked her to state the fact that controlled the decision before consulting the suggested reply. She could then use assistance to examine alternatives and improve the explanation. Afterwards, they compared the response with the decision she had identified.

The sequence mattered. It gave him a view of what she understood, while preserving the tool's useful help. It did not make unaided writing a ritual that every task had to pass. The question was which independent capabilities the role actually required.

If the job requires a person to recognise when to stop, training must establish that recognition. If a reliable tool can perform a calculation the role never needs to reproduce unaided, forcing manual calculation may consume time better spent elsewhere. Independence should follow responsibility, rather than a nostalgia for how the teacher learned.

A lesson costs a piece of today

Northline’s initial plan had been that Maya could ask Shaun whenever she was unsure. After the four-week review and paid handover, his smaller, earlier pattern included scheduled teaching; Nadia covered later cases and served as the alternate supervisor. There was no spare fifth of Shaun’s week waiting to be borrowed.

Peter had two defensible uses for the next available block: shorten the queue of ordinary service requests or let Maya work through exceptions with Shaun. Both helped customers, on different timescales. Shaun could clear the queue faster himself. Maya could not acquire his distinctions by watching it disappear.

Peter protected the teaching block and reduced the routine work scheduled into it. Nadia accepted paid later coverage within her agreed hours; urgent cases went to the designated service cover. Ordinary responses could take longer that day. If the queue began threatening a confirmed promise, they would move the lesson to the next protected slot, record the interruption and reduce intake or buy cover if this recurred. Repeatedly cancelling the lesson would trigger a staffing decision, not become the unrecorded training plan.

That choice does not make learning superior to present service in every case. A commitment that must be kept today can control today’s allocation. The danger is making every day exceptional and discovering, a year later, that the firm still needs somebody experienced.

Let the consequences grow with the evidence

Maya first examined cases before any external message was sent; then she handled a limited category with a supervisor available and her decisions reviewed afterwards; and cases outside that scope stayed with an experienced person, so that at no point was her authority larger than the evidence about what she could already do.

The progression allowed her to encounter real work without making the customer responsible for discovering the limits of her training. It also prevented her from remaining permanently in simulated exercises where every condition had been selected for convenience.

At the next review, the awkward request concerned cartons, not machinery. They were ready, the customer said, but upstairs; nobody would be available to bring them to the agreed collection point. The suggested reply treated “ready” as sufficient. Maya asked who would move them before the vehicle arrived. She had recognised the same distinction beneath different goods and different wording: readiness for the customer was not yet readiness for the promised service.

The customer arranged to have the cartons brought down. Maya confirmed that arrangement with dispatch and then sent the collection answer. Shaun widened her authority to handle comparable readiness questions under the existing terms. Work involving additional handling still needed a separate decision.

Good apprenticeship gradually makes the learner's reasoning and action dependable under a wider range of conditions. The tools can participate in that development. They should not make the development invisible.

Teaching can follow the question

They were examining recurring instruction problems in a set of customer records. Maya had found a useful way to group similar notes. It made patterns visible without reading every entry from the beginning. Dennis recognised that some identical phrases referred to different working conditions.

“You've put all the ready ones together,” Dennis said.

“That was the idea.”

He pointed to an entry. “These are packed. That one still needs somebody to release it.”

Maya split the group. Then she showed him the wording “awaiting stores approval” in several records he had kept elsewhere. Different phrases described the same missing release.

“I wouldn't have put those together,” he said.

“The words don't have to match.”

“Neither do the jobs.”

Experience and familiarity with a new method do not always arrive in the same person. An established practitioner may understand the situation deeply while a newcomer knows a more useful way to investigate it. A younger employee may lack the tool knowledge another person assumes they have. An older employee may be the most fluent user in the team.
