Peter wrote an expectation: “For this customer, prototype shipments will grow before recurring freight. Offer flexibility for small consignments; do not buy a larger regular block yet.” The mechanism was increased attempts meeting an unchanged physical gate. The first paid prototype orders supported the early part of that expectation. They said nothing yet about production growth.

He separated evidence against the forecast from a signal to change the commitment. If the customer began rejecting more designs through a trusted digital screen before ordering samples, physical shipments might decline, weakening his expectation. If prototype orders quickly converted into repeated production orders, the expected sequence could still be right while his decision to defer regular capacity needed to change. Getting the direction right would not excuse missing the pace.

My broader expectation is that work with cheap, representative feedback will permit faster cycles of improvement than work whose useful feedback requires scarce physical trials or long-lived consequences. That does not rank whole industries or guarantee autonomous replacement. It gives a leader a reason to examine the cost and delay of feedback. It would weaken in a particular setting if the supposedly cheap feedback proved a poor guide to the real outcome, or if the physical testing constraint itself became much cheaper.

Beyond Northline

Peter's forecast joins a capability to a customer's work and then to a freight decision. That is useful, but it is still one path. The preface promises principles that can survive several directions of technological change. To keep that promise, I need to ask what happens to a plan when the capability itself refuses to follow its expected path.

Start with a commitment you are considering: hiring people, signing a contract, funding development or telling a team which work it must learn. Write the expectation about AI that makes the commitment sensible. Then put it through four conditions. These are alternatives to prepare for; none needs a date attached to it.

The capability improves faster than your plan allows. A task you expected to protect a margin becomes widely available, or a system becomes dependable at work you had assigned permanently to review. The improvement can open a better service and weaken the account that funds the old one. Find the sentence in your plan that means it cannot do this. State the evidence that would make you retire it, and prepare an alternative use for the resources you would otherwise keep defending.

The capability stalls. The next version does not supply the missing reliability. You have already spent the integration budget, deferred teaching an awkward task or promised a staffing pattern that depends on fewer exceptions. Ask whether the present capability, at its demonstrated level, earns the continuing cost. If it does, use it. If it does not, repeated appeals to the next release are a reason to reconsider the commitment, not evidence for extending it. Keep the people and route needed to perform the work that still exists.

The price changes materially. The system remains equally useful but becomes dearer to operate. A service priced around today's input charge may no longer support the same promise. An alternative provider may be cheaper before, and more expensive after, the cost of moving. This is the complements argument arriving through procurement: having access to a capability is different from controlling the terms on which your organisation can continue to use it. Recalculate the offer and test the exit while you can still afford both choices.

The direction surprises you. Suppose better screening removes the need for physical prototypes instead of merely multiplying them, or customers use assistance to avoid a transaction your forecast expected them to complete more often. The tool can perform better while the demand you prepared for goes away. Preserve contact with the customer outcome, not just the benchmark that encouraged the original investment. You need to notice when a more capable system is answering a different question from the one your business planned to sell.

A plan can fail because the capability outruns it, because the hoped-for improvement never arrives, because an unchanged service becomes expensive, or because customers find a different way to meet the need, and each condition asks you to stop a different kind of spending. One contingency labelled “AI risk” will hide those differences.

You do not need four complete strategies. You need to know which commitment becomes wrong first, what useful work remains and who deserves an early account of the change. Use If the conditions change to put those answers beside your own expectation. A person asked to learn new work should not discover, after investing the effort, that the organisation never wrote down what its plan depended on.

Follow the change into the customer's work

For the professional practice, assistance could change document preparation quickly. The number of engagements might remain constrained by demand, qualified review or the client's willingness to proceed. A faster document would matter to Northline only if it changed the timing, the volume or the nature of the physical work, and the document alone could not establish that change, because the consignment still had to be packed by someone, collected by someone and received by someone at the other end.

For the software customer, new tools could alter team organisation, premises and purchasing. Northline needed to observe the business consequences rather than treating a code benchmark as a freight forecast.

These were fictional customer situations, but the forecasting method is portable. Trace the capability through the customer's work until it reaches the decision relevant to your business. Identify the alternatives and the signals that distinguish them.

Setting Possible early movement Condition for a larger change Useful signal
Repeated digital service Faster assistance on familiar requests Reliable handling of the remaining cases and viable staffing Completed outcomes, recovery work and paid effort
Product development More designs or better early screening Physical validation and demand for the resulting product Prototype orders that progress to paid production
Consequential professional work Assistance with parts of a case Evidence, authority and a workable service arrangement Deployment outcomes under the intended conditions
Cross-firm operations Easier information exchange Compatible terms, capacity and exception decisions Accepted transactions completed without hidden repair

The table is a set of conditional paths, not a timetable or an industry ranking.

Look for a threshold you can name

Some transitions are gradual. Others may accelerate when several requirements become available together. Better capability, lower cost, usable records and an agreed decision route can arrive one at a time and then turn an awkward pilot into a practical operation quite quickly, which is why naming the threshold in advance matters: it lets you compare what you expected with what changed, rather than invent an explanation after the decision has paid off. At Northline, a handover became easier when customers supplied compatible information and both carriers had a clear way to accept or refuse. The company could identify the work removed. It did not need to invoke an inevitable exponential curve to explain the improvement.

A threshold can also move away. Demand may weaken, a provider may change its price or terms, a failure may reveal that the earlier evidence was thinner than it looked, and a regulator, a procurement requirement or a professional body may require a different route altogether, and every one of these is part of the adoption path rather than an external annoyance the forecast is entitled to ignore.

Peter had to distinguish a delay in reaching the same destination from evidence that the destination was wrong. A project repeatedly requiring exceptions to its commercial assumptions may need a different offer. A capability improving while the relevant demand disappears may no longer justify investment.

Peter's forecast therefore contained actions as well as expectations. Prepare an option, expand an existing service, investigate a customer need, defer owned capacity or stop an unsuitable proposal. A forecast that cannot alter a decision is mostly a description of the speaker's confidence.

Let evidence change the map

Keep a short forecast record: what you expect, why, which decision hangs on it, and what you would have to see to move the commitment earlier, later or off the agenda entirely. Then read it again when the signal changes, before you have decided what the signal means. Avoid rewriting the original expectation after the result so that every outcome appears anticipated, which is the most natural thing in the world to do and the surest way to make sure a forecast record teaches you nothing, since a record that is always right has stopped being a record and become a mirror.

Northline developed a limited offer for customers whose irregular work was increasing and held back on a larger capacity commitment. It continued improving the ordinary services already earning their place. Different parts of the business moved at different speeds because the evidence supported different decisions.

Peter kept the prototype offer available and deferred the larger regular transport block. The manufacturer's next paid production order would matter more to that decision than a claim that manufacturing was being transformed.

A provisional map can support a definite commitment. It must also tell you when to move.

Notes

[1] Karpathy, “Verifiability,” 2025, an attributed mechanism hypothesis.

[2] Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, QJE, 2025, studied customer-support setting.

[3] METR, “We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design,” 24 February 2026. Later estimates are not presented here as a definitive speedup.

[4] Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence, Nature, 2025. Text-based simulated consultations do not establish routine clinical outcomes.

23. Who Gets the Abundance?

Dennis wanted some of the gain in his pay. Ava wanted it in the recovery reserve. Peter had a distributor's offer on his desk that would require more money before it earned any.

None of them needed the figures explained again.

The compact workshop service was continuing at 28 customers. Cooperation with Elise's adjoining carrier had opened a limited new reach. Routine work had become easier, though some of the remaining work was harder, and a larger distributor now wanted priority and exclusivity in return for access to recurring volume. Northline's booking supplier had also proposed new commercial terms. An improvement in the operation had become an invitation to negotiate over its proceeds.

Dennis watched Ava move a page out of the distributor pack and put the recovery account on top.

“There's always another page before ours,” he said.

“This page is how we pay when a collection goes wrong.”

“I know what it's for.”

She stopped explaining it.

Three different accounts

Access to assistance, value created and income retained need separate accounts. A tool can spread quickly without improving much work, create substantial value without making its immediate user any richer, and increase a firm's margin while making a customer's experience or an employee's day worse; those results need separate accounts, because a record of who used the tool cannot tell you who gained from the work or who paid for the gain.

Consider a defined observation period: Northline's four-week compact-service trial. Twenty-eight workshops paid for the offer. That is service uptake among the customers approached, not a measure of AI adoption across the region. Their repeated use established that a common collection day could be useful enough to buy. Northline did not measure the money value of every hour customers no longer spent chasing a vehicle, and should not invent that number now.

Ava's model left $280 a week after the defined service costs and central overhead allocation. Four weeks at that level would produce $1,120, still short of the separate $4,800 spent setting up the offer. Even that comparison was a model, not cash she could distribute. She needed the actual collections, costs and outstanding bills before telling Dennis what was available. The full calculation is in the working page on service economics.

The account says nothing by itself about changes in employee earnings or the supplier's margin. Shaun's reduced weekly pay arose from his reduced hours in a separately negotiated staffing change; Nadia's later coverage was voluntary and paid. Neither should be hidden inside a claim that everybody had become more productive.

To examine the distribution over Northline's next operating period, Ava would track the service's actual paying customers and completed collections; customer price, reliability and reported coordination burden; paid hours and earnings in the affected roles; and the cash Northline retained after the costs of providing, maintaining and recovering the offer. She could record what Northline paid its supplier. She could not turn that invoice into knowledge of the supplier's profit.

These measures have different units because they describe different things. Completed collections can improve while employee earnings stay still and supplier charges rise, so the account must allow those movements to appear together instead of asking an adoption count to represent everybody's experience of the gain.

The strongest case for broad gains

Elise thought Peter was giving the large firms too much of the future before they had earned it.

“Your workshops have more choice now,” she said. “So do mine. If we can both offer the service, why does the software company get to keep all of that?”

Her objection deserves its strongest form. When a useful capability becomes widely available, more suppliers can attempt a service. Buyers who can understand the completed result, compare credible offers and move without losing essential records may obtain lower prices, better terms or access they previously lacked. Suppliers can be squeezed precisely because the technology has worked. A buyer's gain and a producer's disappointing margin can be two views of the same improvement.

Northline's compact offer is already a counterexample to a story in which only the technology provider benefits. Small workshops have obtained an affordable service. Elise has obtained paid ordinary work while keeping her company. Those fictional outcomes do not measure an economy, but they expose a logical mistake: a provider's strong position does not imply that nobody else can gain.

Workers can also receive more than instructions to become adaptable. If demand for an improved service grows and experienced people remain necessary to supply it, employers may compete for their capability. A person who can evaluate unfamiliar cases, teach colleagues or connect a new system to an actual operation may gain better pay or greater discretion. Credible alternatives matter: another employer willing to hire, a realistic route into independent work, or an arrangement through which employees bargain together can change what an employer must offer to retain the contribution.

Gain-sharing or shared ownership can make the route more explicit. They still need terms: which gains count, what costs are deducted, who can inspect the account and what happens in a bad period. A promise to share “the upside” can postpone the disagreement until the upside arrives. A defined arrangement gives people something to rely on, though it cannot manufacture a gain where the economics do not support one.

Firms can retain a return too. A common tool does not make Northline and every other carrier identical. Northline has customer relationships, a workable collection pattern and people who know when an ordinary-looking request changes the job. If those contributions remain scarce and useful, customers may pay for them even as the cost of preparing the booking falls. Competence in completing the service can be a source of differentiation; owning a subscription is rarely sufficient evidence of one.

Elise's case becomes strongest where alternatives remain practical at several levels. Customers can leave the carrier, carriers can change software, and workers can take their capability elsewhere. Competition then has routes through which to pass benefits on. A forecast of inevitable concentration would miss those routes and might encourage a leader to surrender negotiating ground unnecessarily.

What could interrupt that route

The same assistance can be available to many participants while something else needed to earn from it remains difficult to obtain: a customer channel, infrastructure, capital, operating capacity or a necessary agreement. These are the complements. The useful question is who controls them and what another participant must accept to gain access.

The distributor controlled volume Northline wanted. The booking supplier supplied a service whose replacement would consume time. Northline controlled local relationships and limited capacity to fulfil promises. Elise controlled resources in her own area. Each could offer something the others could not obtain merely by asking a more capable model.

The supplier's bargaining position depended partly on the cost of changing it. Thomas's usable export reduced one cost. It did not eliminate testing, transition work or the risk of disrupting customers. The distributor's proposed exclusivity would create a different dependence by limiting Northline's independent customer relationships. An attractive initial volume could make a later refusal more expensive.

My expectation is conditional: widespread access to capable assistance can coexist with a narrow distribution of retained income when a few participants control these necessary complements and alternatives are costly to use. I would look for that mechanism before assuming that the people adopting the tool will retain a proportionate share of its benefits. The claim is about the conditions governing the share, not a race between an adoption percentage and a quantity of money.

The broad-gains case changes the expectation when it changes those conditions. Several credible suppliers, readable records, manageable transition effort and customers able to compare completed outcomes can weaken the provider's claim. Workers' scarce capabilities and credible employment alternatives can strengthen theirs. A technology that makes a complement abundant can undo power previously built on controlling it.

Ava could test part of this account in her own negotiation. Were alternative offers usable after including transition work? Did their presence improve the terms Northline could obtain? Were savings from routine work surviving in the service account, or leaving through higher input charges? Were customers getting a better offer while Northline's retained return fell?

Contrary evidence matters. If the supplier repeatedly reduced effective charges and improved terms despite Northline's high switching costs, dependence alone would be an inadequate explanation of the bargain. If customers had comparable offers and practical exit but received no improvement, she would need to examine demand, capacity or distinctions the comparison had missed. If worker earnings and autonomy rose as services expanded, that would challenge a prediction that gains would bypass employees. An account of power should make these observations interesting, not explain them away.

A reserve is somebody else's postponed gain

Dennis and Ava agreed that recovery needed funding. Their dispute concerned who should wait while it was rebuilt.

For this allocation decision the board identified a small amount of cash remaining after already incurred costs, committed pay and provision for the continuing service. It was not the model's entire contribution. There was enough to strengthen the recovery provision or make an immediate discretionary employee payment; doing both at the proposed level would require deferring another funded commitment. No new numerical amount was assumed.

Dennis preferred a smaller payment now and a slower replenishment. Employees had supplied the operating knowledge and borne the disruption. A visible share would acknowledge that contribution at the point the business began benefiting. Ava preferred retaining the available amount because another recovery could otherwise require cutting already planned work. Both alternatives served people. They served different people at different times, with different exposure if the next month went badly.

Peter asked whether the distributor's prospective volume could cover the gap. Ava refused to count an unsigned arrangement as available cash. Funding that development now was a third claim, not an answer to the first two.

The board, which held authority over the allocation and exposure, chose to retain the available amount for recovery and continued operation. It deferred a general discretionary increase and further development spending against those proceeds. Existing agreed pay, including Nadia's additional coverage, remained a cost to honour, not a reserve to borrow from.

The reconsideration point was the next closed monthly operating account. Before that review, Ava would show the actual cash retained, recovery spending, unpaid customer balances and the provision required to support the already accepted work. If the agreed recovery provision had been restored and cash remained after those commitments, the board would consider a defined employee payment before a new discretionary expansion. If the account still fell short, it would name the shortfall and the work being protected. A future review was no guarantee of a payment, but it now had evidence to produce and a decision to make.

Dennis asked for his preference for an earlier partial payment to remain alongside the decision. It did. He had not failed to understand prudence; he had assigned a different weight to delayed compensation. Nor did Ava's chosen priority prove that every further reserve demand would be justified. A reserve without a purpose and a review can become a permanent name for money that will never be shared.

Three places to act

Some decisions can be made inside the organisation, others require agreement with someone free to refuse, and a third class requires institutions able to hear claims no single firm can settle; knowing which kind of decision you face changes what it means to act.

Some choices were Northline's to make directly. Its board could choose this allocation, give employees a usable account and fund the next review. It could not describe a discretionary payment as inevitable or turn agreed wages into a residual share of whatever remained.

Other choices required negotiation. Peter refused the distributor's broad exclusivity and offered to examine paid priority for a defined quantity of capacity. That protected independent customer relationships while leaving a route to new work. The distributor had alternatives; Northline might lose the opportunity. Shaun still feared that paid priority would gradually make the small accounts inconvenient through the ordinary drift of attention towards whoever was paying most, while Peter believed that explicit reservations could fund capacity without displacing the promises already made, and neither of them could prove it yet, which gave the proposed cap a job beyond making the agreement easier to sign. The proposed expansion still required board approval. Agreement on a cap would not settle Shaun's concern by itself.

A third class of choices required institutions beyond Northline. One carrier could maintain an export; it could not make every supplier accept a portable account. Peter could contribute paid operating examples to shared standards work and accept other firms' authority to contest the definitions. Effective rules for competition, employment transitions or widely used infrastructure required broader representation and public decisions. A company could participate in that work without appointing itself governor of the market.

Beyond Northline

Peter can bring an operating example and pay for someone to examine it. He cannot make a regional market accept his definition. That limit is easy to respect in fiction, where another firm has a name and a voice. It is harder when the people who should contest the arrangement are absent from the room.

I do not mean that public protections must all be invented from nothing. The EU's General Data Protection Regulation provides safeguards for specified categories of solely automated decisions, including human intervention and contestation in certain cases.[1] That is a scoped legal provision, not a universal right covering every use of an algorithm. Its existence is also a reason to reject the claim that the only available choices are a company's goodwill or helplessness.

The operating questions remain concrete. Can a person identify the decision, obtain the relevant record and reach someone able to reconsider it? What happens to the lost shift, pending application or withheld service while that takes place? A right, a contact address and a funded route through a disputed case do different work. A leader should find out which are already required and which are actually available before claiming to have supplied a remedy.

Portability has a similar distinction. Sending someone a file is a start. Making it usable elsewhere may require agreed meanings, documented limits and a receiving institution willing to accept it. Privacy, confidentiality and the other people's information inside a record constrain what can properly travel. Those are reasons to design a workable transfer, not to assume either unrestricted sharing or permanent captivity is the answer.

Nor can Northline's private decision about a vacancy settle the terms of a labour-market transition. An employer, a union or worker representative, a training provider and a public agency may need to examine different parts of the same change: what work remains, what experience a new role requires, who can attend the training and who pays while somebody learns. An employee should not have to become an expert negotiator merely to discover which promise applies to them.

This work can begin with a very small contribution. Pay for a worker representative's time to examine a proposed measure. Bring a documented failure to a standards group. Ask an industry association to test an export with a receiving supplier. Give a regulator an operating account that includes the cases in which your preferred rule would be inconvenient. Participation means allowing that account to change the proposed rule, including when the change costs your own organisation something.

Boards belong in this picture too. Miriam's responsibility cannot stop at scrutinising Peter. A board that authorised a budget or accepted an assurance needs to examine what its own choice made possible, and give the people carrying its consequences a usable account of why it would decide differently next time. Adding a reviewer above each reviewer cannot remove the need for that answer.

There will be disagreements you cannot resolve and institutions you cannot repair. I cannot tell you from these pages which table you should join. I can ask you to distinguish a decision outside your authority from work outside your concern. Name one arrangement your own plan relies on, find out who can legitimately change it, and decide what evidence, money or participation you are prepared to contribute.

Bring the decision back within reach

The distinction gives leadership a practical reach. Choose the terms you actually control, being clear about where that authority ends; negotiate where the other party has a legitimate choice, which means accepting that they may use it; and help build the arrangements that no single bargain can supply, even when the work takes you beyond your own organisation and gives you no final say. Each route has costs and each has opponents, and none of the three is replaced by saying that the technology will distribute its own benefits, because that sentence gives nobody an obligation, names nobody who can challenge the result, and leaves the person still waiting for a share with nothing they can use.

The distributor's reply had not arrived when the allocation meeting ended. Ava left the next review date on the account. Dennis took a copy. He would want the actual figures then, not another explanation of why reserves mattered.

Note

[1] Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 22, especially paragraphs 1–3. The provision concerns solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, includes exceptions and specifies safeguards; paragraph 3 applies to the cases in paragraph 2(a) and (c). This example is not a statement that every AI-assisted decision attracts the same rights or a guide to any reader's legal obligations.

Section VIII · Transmitting

Accountability in promises, words, and rewards

24. The Name on the Work

Peter's name appeared beneath a statement that was true in a narrower sense than the board understood.

Northline's partner handover process had been tested. Ordinary consignments had moved successfully between Northline and Elise's carrier. The record of acceptance was useful, and both companies had earned money from work they could complete under the agreed terms.

The distributor now offered a larger, bounded programme. It had withdrawn the broad exclusivity demand Peter had rejected. The new proposal reserved capacity for defined work and could justify a more substantial commercial commitment.

Peter's recommendation said: “The handover process is proven. The proposed volume fits the reserved capacity.” Both sentences had a basis. Together they invited the board to treat the larger programme as more of the same.

The programme also permitted a same-day change of collection point among listed distributor sites, subject to both carriers confirming the revision. Ordinary partner trials had used settled locations. Peter had not established how often those revisions would arrive, how long agreement would take, or what recovery would consume when the remaining windows stopped fitting.

Miriam brought the recommendation to the board. The board approved the larger bounded test on the basis of the operating account, including Peter's assurance. He had not acted outside the formal approval. The failure lay in the evidence the approval was understood to represent.

No senior person can personally inspect everything a complex organisation produces. Work arrives through employees, partners, systems and suppliers. An approval necessarily relies on other contributions.

What has been examined? Under which conditions? Which unresolved assumptions remain? What authority does the approver possess, and what resources support the commitment? A signature that leaves these questions unclear can turn a limited success into a broader assurance without anyone ever stating the extra claim directly, which is how an organisational overstatement can be made without an explicit lie: a name is placed under a sentence that was true in a room and false in the building.

He was not the only person responsible for asking: the board could have demanded a more specific account, Thomas could describe the system's tested scope, and Sunder and Elise knew the operational boundaries, but those contributions had not been brought together before the signature in an account precise enough for the decision.

The work exceeded the reassuring description

The distributor requested a move from one listed collection site to another, a request permitted inside the approved programme. The goods and volume were permitted. The revision still needed acceptance by both carriers; the original confirmed collection remained due. Northline could reach the new site, but doing so would miss Elise's original handover window.

Elise offered a later handover. By the time the distributor confirmed the site was ready, that alternative no longer fitted her remaining route. While examining the request, Northline had asked the customer to wait and held its original dispatch movement. The customer had left the original collection available. Northline failed to release that movement before its last usable window passed. Checking the revision had consumed the time needed to honour the commitment that still stood.

Sunder could see the unresolved status. What he could not supply from the shared screen was another handover window. Recovering the distributor's already accepted underlying commitment now required a separate movement. Similar revisions arrived while the team was resolving this one. The numerical cap remained intact; the coordination assumption did not.

Northline paid for additional recovery work. Elise's team did too, and the costs had to be reconciled rather than silently absorbed by the partner. Some collections were missed. One small workshop, whose ordinary promise should have remained dependable, lost its scheduled collection because the recovery work consumed capacity the company had not adequately protected.

The customer did not care that Northline had respected the distributor programme's numerical cap. The goods had not moved as promised.

Peter called the result a failure of the approved design. He did not attribute it to employees failing to adopt the system or to a partner being insufficiently flexible. Those explanations would have protected the recommendation by moving its omitted work onto someone else's character.

The letter on Nadia’s screen

“We recognise the disruption caused by the recent changes to our partner programme and are taking steps to prevent a recurrence.”

The draft went on to describe the capacity conflict and named a person to contact. The workshop owner had already contacted that person. Her goods were still beside the door.

Nadia read the letter again from the point of view of someone standing beside packed goods, waiting to know whether to call another carrier. Much of the explanation could wait. The status of the collection could not.

Nadia obtained those facts before improving the prose. Dispatch could arrange a separate collection through an available carrier. Northline would pay the agreed collection charge. The delivery timing still needed confirmation from the onward arrangement, so the customer should not yet repeat the original promise.

Peter approved the recovery expense through the relevant operating authority. He did not ask Nadia to describe the company as committed to making things right while leaving the cost undecided.

Nadia replaced the opening:

“We missed your scheduled collection. I have arranged a separate collection for this afternoon, which Northline will pay for. I cannot yet confirm the delivery time, so please do not rely on the original delivery promise. I will return to you by three with the latest position, even if I am still waiting for the answer. You can reply directly to me here.”

She checked the time with dispatch before sending it. Three o’clock was a commitment she would have to keep whether or not the news was reassuring.

Nadia used assistance to shorten the explanation and check whether the sequence was clear. She retained responsibility for the facts, including the carrier arrangement and the time of the next answer. A fluent sentence about resolving the matter promptly would have been less useful than the actual commitment she could honour.

Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang's 2023 experiment with 453 college-educated professionals offers a useful comparison. Participants undertook incentivised professional writing tasks; random access to ChatGPT improved the writing-task productivity the researchers measured.[1] That is evidence for a real component benefit. It does not show that an organisation had made the promise described in a well-written message. Nadia's problem required an authorised recovery before it required better prose.

My starting point is to know the truth and communicate it simply. Neither half can substitute for the other. Nadia cannot write a usable promise until Northline has decided what it will pay for; once that decision exists, the customer should not have to excavate it from a paragraph about the company’s values.

The alternative collection could not restore the workshop owner's lost time or guarantee her own customer would accept a revised delivery. Northline should say what it could repair without turning its response into a claim that the harm was complete and neatly reversible.

Peter considered calling the workshop owner himself. A call from the person running the company might communicate the seriousness of the failure. It could also become another conversation in which she had to repeat the facts to someone who would later pass the work back to Nadia.

He asked what would help. Nadia was already holding the case and could obtain the remaining answer. They agreed that Peter would be available if a decision exceeded her authority, while she remained the customer's contact.

For some recipients, a written account is more useful than a call. They can read it at the relevant time, share it with a colleague and return to the exact terms. Others need a conversation to clarify an unfamiliar choice. Some need an accessible format or help in another language. The form should serve the person and the decision, rather than the speaker's preferred way to appear attentive.

Nadia sent the revised letter and spoke with the owner when she had a moment.

“I can get them out of here this afternoon,” the owner said. “That helps. But I have already told my customer they were on their way.”

Nadia started to explain the capacity conflict, then stopped. The owner had not asked for the explanation again.

“Do you need something in writing to send them?”

“I need a delivery time.”

“I know. I don’t have it yet. I’ll call you at three.”

Nadia removed an internal term for the capacity conflict because it added no useful meaning for the owner. She kept the distinction between a confirmed collection and an unconfirmed delivery time even though it made the letter less reassuring. The recipient needed that uncertainty in order to avoid making another unsupported promise.

When producing messages becomes easier, organisations can send more of them. If each new status produces a fresh explanation, reassurance and invitation to respond, the recipient must work through an expanding correspondence to find the one changed fact that requires a decision. Their attention has become part of the service cost.

Northline kept the collection case in one coherent thread and made the changed status visible. It did not send a fresh generic reassurance each time a system updated a record. The customer could follow what had changed and what had not yet been confirmed.

At 2:58, Nadia still had no delivery time. She opened the message she had sent earlier: I will return to you by three with the latest position, even if I am still waiting for the answer.

It had been an easier sentence to write than it was to keep. She checked the onward carrier's response again. Nothing.

At three, she called.

“You've got a time?” the owner asked.

“Not yet.”

Silence.

“Then why are you calling?”

Nadia moved the prepared explanation away from the centre of her screen.

“Because I said I would.”

“All right,” the owner said. “I'm here.”

They agreed that Nadia would return by four if the answer had not arrived sooner. She obtained the delivery information before then and called again. The owner could finally give her customer a revised account and decide whether it was acceptable. The separate collection proceeded at Northline's expense.

The owner wanted the normal collection to work the following week. Nadia wrote that down without marking the relationship restored.

Answer for what your name allowed

The board review separated the operational record from the explanation Peter wanted to give about his intentions. Which commitments had been made? What had failed? Who had carried the cost? Which parts of the assurance had evidence behind them?

Peter acknowledged that his wording had invited broader reliance than the test supported. The board acknowledged that its review had accepted that account without obtaining the missing operational evidence. Miriam recorded both conclusions.

They stopped further enlargement of the programme while completing or repairing existing obligations. The company funded customer recovery and reconciled the additional partner work. Nobody was asked to erase paid hours to make the original forecast appear closer to the result.

Then the board changed the launch authority. Further activation of expanded partner categories required a written operating-readiness account from Sunder and Elise for their respective parts, a financial account from Ava and explicit board approval. The people supplying those accounts received time and the authority to identify a condition as unmet. Their names would not be added as ceremonial safeguards beneath Peter's recommendation.

Peter could continue developing opportunities. He could no longer activate the relevant expansion on the strength of the earlier broad readiness assurance, even within money already earmarked. The restriction concerned a defined decision, not an unexplained removal of his whole role.

Miriam did not acquire a private veto. She organised the board's review under the agreed governance arrangement. The board retained the decision and had to make its reasoning answerable too.

The failure had crossed several organisations. Northline sold the service, Elise supplied part of its execution and the distributor shaped the incoming work. The booking provider supported a routine function but had not promised to resolve every operating conflict in the expanded partnership.

Confusing those roles would make repair harder. Northline could not blame the booking vendor for an authority gap between carriers. Elise could not be expected to honour a customer promise she had never accepted. The distributor's desire for responsiveness did not create unlimited capacity at either firm.

The recipient and the board needed different answers. The owner needed to know what would happen to her goods. The board needed to establish what Peter’s assurance had allowed, why its own review had accepted it, and which part of his authority had to change. A better apology could not perform that institutional work; a thorough board review could not collect the cartons.

Beyond Northline

Northline can fund a separate collection and change the authority behind its next promise. It cannot return the workshop owner's lost time. The scene already puts a limit on repair, but it does not take us to the stakes at which a corrected record can arrive after the harm has become permanent.

A discharge instruction can be acted on before it is corrected; a safeguarding decision can leave a person exposed; a load calculation can permit construction that others will occupy; and an apparently routine assessment can consume the last margin of time or money available to the person whose case it closes. The output leaves the screen as somebody else's action.

These are possible consequences in different domains, not interchangeable examples of one approval process. Clinical care, structural engineering and safeguarding have different evidence, authority and professional obligations. A bounded commercial test in this book does not authorise experimentation on the people relying on those protections.

I chose an ordinary business so that we could inspect the mechanism closely. Ordinary logistics can itself involve serious safety risks; this story has concentrated on commercial and organisational decisions. Its recoverable mistakes are a limit of the illustration, not a reason to assume yours will be recoverable too.

If you work where the result cannot readily be undone, begin earlier than the apology. Identify the point after which withdrawing the answer would no longer prevent the consequence. Ask what evidence is needed before that point, who is qualified and authorised to decide, and what the service does when that evidence is unavailable. Sometimes the supported action is to preserve an existing safe arrangement; sometimes delay is itself dangerous and an established emergency procedure must govern the response.

I cannot supply those domain decisions. I can insist that the cheaper production of an assurance should not quietly lower the evidence needed to rely on it. Before putting your name on the work, imagine the recipient has already acted. What would you need to have established while there was still time?

A limit means something when it costs an opportunity

Before the additional readiness work was complete, the distributor offered another tranche of business on a short decision window. Peter believed Northline could handle it with the revised attention now being applied. He wanted permission to proceed while finishing the remaining exercise.

Sunder could not yet support the account of the exception load. Elise agreed. Ava could show the commercial attraction but not make the missing operating condition true.

The board declined activation. The distributor placed that work elsewhere.

The board might prove too cautious in a later case. It would need to examine that possibility through evidence, rather than assume every refusal wise. For this decision, the agreed condition was unmet and the promise would not be made.

Peter reread the sentence about proven handovers. He could still defend the words one at a time. He crossed out the sentence.

Note

[1] Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang, Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence, Science, 2023. Preregistered randomised online writing experiment; the published sample is 453. The earlier preprint reports a different sample. No organisational income or completed-service effect is inferred here.

25. What You Tolerate

The launch summary looked better than the week had felt.

Thomas's summary showed twelve of twelve handover records completed. Ava put the service account beside it. Three of those twelve had needed further calls or paid partner coordination; one of the three had missed its promised collection before being recovered. The technical count was true. The heading, “Programme completions,” let it answer a different question.

“Which twelve?” Ava asked.

“The transfers.”

“Then say transfers. This one was still waiting for us.”

These are fictional counts from a review sample, separate from the workshop-service financial model. The costs of the calls and recovery sat in other records, where a reader of Thomas's summary would not see them.

He knew the distinction mattered. He also knew that the company wanted evidence that the larger partner programme was becoming manageable after its failed expansion. He had worked hard on the system and did not consider every downstream dispute a software failure.

That was a defensible distinction for diagnosing a component. It was an inadequate account of the service result people thought they were reading.

When Ava reconciled the summary with the recovery costs, the gap became clear. Peter could treat it as a reporting mistake and move on. Or he could examine what Northline had made attractive to report.

People notice what earns approval

An organisation communicates its standards through money, assignments, attention and exceptions. People can read the stated values, watch who receives the next opportunity and notice which inconvenient fact is forgiven in a successful presentation, then reasonably give the repeated decisions more weight than the words. Those decisions are instructions too.

At Northline, visible completion had received praise. Recovery work had often appeared as a cost to explain. Thomas could point to useful improvements he had made, while the work required to finish difficult cases made the programme look less successful.

The pressure did not remove his responsibility for the summary. It helped explain why a technically accurate measure had been allowed to imply a broader result.

Examine both. If the organisation rewards a distorted account, correcting one employee without changing the incentive will leave the next person facing the same temptation. If the leader blames the incentive for everything, individual choices cease to matter.

Peter asked Thomas what he understood readers would infer. Thomas acknowledged that the summary made the operation look more complete than it was. He had expected the other records to qualify it without drawing attention to the gap.

Repair the account and the reason it became attractive

Thomas replaced the headline with three lines: twelve records transferred; nine completed without additional intervention; three required recovery, including one missed promise. All twelve could eventually be closed without making twelve the answer to how many had worked as promised. The people who had relied on the earlier account received the correction. The additional costs remained in the programme's economics rather than being treated as unrelated effort somewhere else in the firm.

Peter also changed what the launch review would recognise. Discovering a recurring exception early and reducing its cost counted as useful progress, and a high completion rate supported by hidden intervention did not, which meant the review was now giving the team a practical reason to make a problem visible while there was still time and authority to do something about it. The team could report a narrower success without having to defend it as a failure to believe in the programme, which gave people a reason to tell the truth about the pilot before its limits became somebody else's surprise.

For a period, Thomas's expanded-programme summaries received a second review before they supported consequential decisions. He retained his technical work and the resources required to correct the account. The restriction addressed the reporting choice; it was not a public performance of punishment.

Peter's earlier assurance to the board remained in the same record. He could not demand a standard of evidence from Thomas while treating his own overstatement as a visionary error beyond ordinary scrutiny.

Distinguish an error from concealment

People will make mistakes in a changing operation. Some arise from missing information, unfamiliar work or a reasonable judgment that proves wrong. Others involve knowingly suppressing a fact someone needs. The response should depend on what happened.

If every error receives punishment, people have a reason to hide the early signs of failure; if every deliberate concealment receives forgiveness, the colleague who reports a problem bears a cost the person hiding it avoids. Neither arrangement produces a dependable account of the work.

Investigate the situation before assigning the category. What information did the person have? What did they understand others would rely on? Could they raise the problem safely? What choices did they make after becoming aware of it?

Thomas had not invented a successful handover. He had allowed a narrow count to function as a broader success claim. The appropriate response included correction, a review of the relevant reporting authority and a change in the measure's use. If the same deliberate omission recurred, it would require a different decision about his responsibility.

The exception teaches the rule

A leader may say that staff should report problems and then make one damaging exception for a highly valued performer. The exception can become the most informative part of the policy.

Thomas was useful to Northline. He had removed real work, helped create a viable service and learned to buy capability when that was better than building it. Those contributions mattered. They did not entitle him to shape the operating account around the results he preferred.

Equally, the mistake did not erase the contributions. Peter could name the conduct without rewriting Thomas as the cause of the whole programme's failure.

Standards travel through commercial terms

Northline's internal repair exposed a similar problem across the partner relationship. Elise's carrier had performed additional coordination that was difficult to represent in the routine handover price. If Northline rewarded only apparently frictionless work, the partner had reason to absorb or obscure that effort until it became intolerable.

The firms revised their reporting and payment arrangement for exceptions. Work outside the ordinary category had to be named by whoever noticed it, accepted by whoever it was done for, and paid for under an agreement that made its cost visible to the company receiving it. Reporting a problem promptly would not itself trigger a penalty designed for failing to perform an accepted commitment. Deliberate concealment remained a different matter.

This was not unlimited permission to bill for any inconvenience. The parties needed evidence and a decision route. It made visible work easier to settle without rewarding the appearance that it had never existed.

Such terms can spread a standard beyond one company's walls. A buyer's procurement rules influence what suppliers find economical to disclose. A customer's insistence on impossible response times can push uncertainty into another organisation's unrecorded labour. A platform's definitions can shape what many participants count as success.

Leaders therefore transmit culture partly through the agreements they impose on others, and those agreements can travel further than a speech: a procurement clause can reach a supplier's night shift, a response-time requirement can reach a subcontractor's family, and a values statement about transparency means as much as the commercial terms allow it to mean. It means little if those terms punish a supplier for telling the truth about a failing arrangement.

Northline's next review contained a lower-looking completion figure and a clearer account of the service. It also showed a recurring exception that Thomas and Elise's team had reduced through a practical change. Peter praised that improvement without pretending the remaining recovery work had vanished.

Thomas left the recovery line on the page when he sent the next account. It made the number smaller. It made the claim usable.

Section IX · Lasting

Maintained capability, recovery, and independence

26. What Compounds

Before the new coverage arrangements, Northline had an unofficial evening shift.

It began when a phone lit up: Shaun remembering a customer's earlier window, Thomas explaining which record to trust, Sunder settling capacity from his kitchen while colleagues waited for authority nobody had given them.

Nobody scheduled it. Peter encountered it as responsiveness. The people working it encountered it at home.

Then Shaun's hours changed. Northline paid for later cover and assigned authority to those providing it. Some instructions took longer to catch up.

“Ask Shaun,” the old note said.

Nadia looked at the time. Shaun had finished his agreed earlier hours. She was covering customer decisions. The request in front of her concerned a recurring exception, not an emergency requiring somebody to be called back into their working day.

She opened the linked record. It contained the reason for the earlier decision, the conditions that mattered and the authority now assigned to the role. She could obtain the remaining fact and decide within her own scope.

When Sunder came past, she showed him the old instruction.

“Shall we change that?” he asked.

“We already changed the job,” Nadia said. “The note is catching up.”

They retained the useful explanation and removed the obsolete dependency on one person's availability. The customer received an answer without Shaun's private time becoming part of the service.

Beyond Northline

The note made Shaun's evening look available. Changing it helped one ordinary case finish inside somebody else's paid authority. The scene can show that repair. It cannot show every dinner, journey or hour of rest interrupted before the company learned to count the work differently.

You may recognise the arrangement without recognising the job: a colleague who answers a question from the train, a parent who checks a message after a child has gone to sleep, a specialist who briefly opens a laptop because explaining why it must wait feels harder than doing it. No single request appears large enough to deserve a new staffing decision. Together they can make a service depend on a second, unagreed working day.

I want the working pages in this book read with that limit in mind. Even an account that records repair time can miss the interruption around it: the person who must remain reachable cannot quite leave, though the eventual answer may take only a minute. Recording more activity is not the same as understanding what availability costs.

The remedy is not to interrogate employees about private lives or reward the most dramatic account of exhaustion. Examine the work. Which requests arrive outside staffed hours? Which genuinely cannot wait? Who has the authority to answer them, and what cover has actually been agreed? If colleagues choose extra work, the choice needs terms they can understand and a refusal they can safely make.

This applies to the person running the business too. Your willingness to remain available can conceal a decision nobody else has permission to make. There may be a season when that is a conscious bargain. It should have an end or a price you have deliberately accepted.

Name your organisation's unofficial shift. Then ask which part you are paying for, which part you are borrowing and which part exists because an instruction still names the wrong person.

What remains after the output is used

Some work supplies a result and ends there. Other work leaves something behind. The linked record gave Nadia the reason for an earlier decision and the authority to handle this one. Shaun's explanation was still helping customers after his working day had ended. Maya's growing competence and the agreement with Elise offered other ways for today's effort to make tomorrow's work easier.

These effects can build on one another: better context supports a useful tool, the tool releases time to examine a recurring problem, and solving that problem improves the service enough to fund another piece of work that nobody previously had time to begin. Each link still has to hold.

The same record also shows how this goes backwards. “Ask Shaun” had once directed a question to someone who could answer it. After his hours and responsibilities changed, it directed an ordinary case into his private time. Nadia had to separate the useful explanation from the obsolete instruction. The fact that something took effort to create does not establish that it remains an asset.

Maintenance belongs in the account

Ava asked the team what recurring work the new arrangements required. The answer included reviewing service assumptions, maintaining the shared records, paying for supervision and keeping the partner exchange usable when either firm's systems changed.

These costs were not evidence that the improvements had failed. They were part of owning the improvements.

An organisation can make its initial return look stronger by leaving maintenance unspecified. Someone eventually performs the work through spare time, or the asset deteriorates until a failure makes its condition visible. Neither is a dependable investment account.

Retirement is part of maintaining value. Keeping an old rule after its reason has disappeared can consume attention and prevent a better method. The ability to discard is particularly important when generating new material becomes cheap. Otherwise each improvement leaves another layer for the next person to navigate.

Nadia did not preserve “ask Shaun” as a tribute to his expertise. She preserved the part of his work that could help her decide. That was the more useful form of respect.

I care about this test because it asks whether a leader has made other people stronger or simply made themselves harder to do without. I would want my explanation to remain useful when I am unavailable, and easy to correct when it is wrong. That requires leaving the reason with the work and giving someone else permission to act on it. The name on the explanation matters less than the decision it helps them make.

Capability can travel with a person

Maya could now handle a wider set of service decisions than when she first joined. Her authority remained specific, but the evidence supporting it had grown. She had learned through paid supervision, real cases, tools and colleagues who made their distinctions examinable.

The service team benefited from Maya's development. Maya also possessed a capability that could matter elsewhere, and Northline did not own every future use of it merely because it had paid for the supervision through which she acquired it, which is an uncomfortable fact for an employer: training costs money, trained people may leave, and the business has to make an investment whose benefits it cannot entirely keep. A business needs enough return to sustain the investment. It also needs to offer work and terms worth choosing, rather than treating dependence as the only way to retain people.

A person who stays because the organisation remains a good place to contribute is different from a person who cannot take their knowledge anywhere else. The first relationship can support initiative and truthful disagreement. The second may preserve staffing while weakening the qualities the leader claims to value.

Some gains belong between institutions

Elise proposed a small shared set of exception definitions for the carriers using the handover arrangement. Each company kept its own customer records and commercial decisions. They could still agree how to describe a refused request, an accepted commitment and a condition requiring additional authority.

The work would cost both firms time. Its benefits could extend beyond the first pair if other participants used the same distinctions.

Peter initially wanted to keep the definitions inside Northline's own system. Thomas pointed out that the handover became easier when the other party could use the same account without recreating it. Exclusivity would preserve control over a small asset while reducing the benefit of the larger arrangement.

Their first disputed definition was “received.” Northline used it for a request arriving in a system. Elise wanted to reserve it for a person taking responsibility for examining the request. Either meaning worked internally. Across firms it could start a response clock before the other party believed the work had begun.

“If your screen says received at six,” Elise said, “am I already late when we open?”

They separated arrival from acknowledgment and acceptance. The response obligation began under each agreed staffed arrangement, not whenever a machine could record an arrival. Peter accepted the less impressive-looking status because it described what Northline could actually rely on.

Both firms assigned paid maintenance time. A proposed definition change had to show an example and identify the obligation it would alter; neither firm could make the other liable by updating its own software. Until both accepted a revision, the previous shared version governed their exchange. New participants could propose changes on the same terms. They shared operational patterns, with customer confidences removed, rather than pooling customer records. The common asset now had a modest constitution as well as useful words.

Protect future options from today's attractive number

Put Shaun back on the queue during Maya's teaching block and more requests get answered today. The cost appears later, when an unfamiliar case still needs someone she has not learned to replace. Northline's board faced a similar trade with money: pay out the recovery reserve now, and the next failed collection must be funded from elsewhere. Today's account needs to show what tomorrow would have to replace.

The answer is not to preserve every option at any cost. Keeping unused capacity can be wasteful. Training can be badly designed. Relationships can be maintained long after they cease to serve a worthwhile purpose.

The useful account identifies what is being built or spent and why the trade-off fits the situation. It should make depletion visible alongside current output.

Northline's board could see that the larger programme had consumed recovery resources. Continuing the viable compact service and rebuilding the reserve was less exciting than another immediate expansion. It preserved the means to attempt a better version later.

Nadia closed the customer case and changed the obsolete note. Shaun did not receive a message asking him to rescue an ordinary decision after his day had ended. Maya could see the reasoning when a related case came to her later.

She left the useful explanation in the record. The name no longer had to answer the phone.

27. What Breaks

The screen was still open. It had stopped telling them anything useful.

Ordinary booking updates were failing to complete. Thomas checked the local connection, then the service status. The routine booking provider was unavailable. He did not yet know how long the interruption would last.

Nadia had customers waiting for answers. Sunder had confirmed work to dispatch. A customer who had pressed submit could not tell whether the company had accepted a change.

Then Elise called from the partner carrier.

“Have you still got yours?”

She used the same provider for part of her booking operation. The interruption had reached both companies. Their shared handover arrangement had its own records and rules, but the ordinary flow feeding it was impaired on each side.

The plan to ask another operator for help suddenly contained an assumption: that the other operator had remained available.

Beyond Northline

Elise's call removes the comforting assumption that help will arrive from outside. The scene is about to compress choices that earlier chapters had time to examine. You may have four minutes, two missing facts and a person waiting on the line.

I would keep three questions within reach: what must be protected now, what can we reliably do with the people and information available, and who will own the next decision before waiting itself causes harm? They collect the book's attention to consequences, evidence and authority without requiring you to reconstruct its whole argument under pressure.

The fuller comparison belongs afterwards. In clinical, safety or other regulated work, established emergency procedures and qualified authority govern the response; these questions do not replace them. Rehearse the compressed account while you have time. The working page Under pressure is short enough to keep beside the recovery arrangement, where somebody other than you can find it.

Name what you can still do

Sunder began with the commitments Northline could read and support. The company had retained usable customer records outside the unavailable service. Those records gave it an account of confirmed work. They did not provide the speed or capacity of the normal booking process.

He marked the work that could proceed, the cases needing clarification and the requests the company could not responsibly accept. New optional changes would wait. Some new business would receive a refusal rather than an uncertain promise.

“We can do this list,” he told Nadia. “We can't do the normal day by hand.”

The latest rehearsal had retained the limit established after the supplier purchase: the records and associated questions for twelve confirmed collections through a two-hour reduced-operation block. It had not established that the same team could repeat such blocks indefinitely. This was a limit on manual booking and dispatch administration, not a claim that twelve vehicles or deliveries could be completed in two hours. Sunder selected the first twelve supported commitments from the readable record and marked every other case for an answer rather than an assumed acceptance. These are Northline's fictional operating limits, not a recommended staffing ratio.

At the end of the two hours they would reassess the people, pending work and provider status before promising another block. A printed list was useful. Multiplying it by the rest of the day was not evidence.

A dependency can be shared without being visible

Two suppliers with different names may rely on the same infrastructure, and a nominal backup may require the identity service, data connection or specialist whose failure made the primary route unavailable, leaving the organisation with several routes to the same interruption. Independent firms can share a dependency too.

The number of alternatives on a diagram does not establish their independence.

At Northline, the booking supplier was distinct from Elise's company and from the partner handover rules. Yet both carriers' normal intake used the same provider. The companies had diversified operational ownership without eliminating this shared technical dependency.

Thomas and Elise's technical contact compared what remained available. They avoided treating a message from another carrier as confirmation that the original request had completed. Each accepted commitment needed an account both sides could use. The shared definitions developed earlier helped them distinguish confirmed work from requests still in doubt.

A common standard could support recovery even while a common provider caused disruption. Shared arrangements can create resilience or shared exposure depending on what is shared and how it is governed.

Keep the service promise smaller than the recovery fantasy

Peter wanted to preserve the customer experience. He also wanted the team to know that refusing new work was authorised. Otherwise people might interpret commercial pressure as a request to conceal the reduced capacity through extra personal effort.

Paid coverage was rearranged within the actual people available. Shaun helped during his agreed earlier hours and completed a clear handover to Nadia. His reduced working arrangement did not silently expand because the company faced a difficult day. Additional work required an explicit paid agreement with someone able to provide it.

Dennis helped identify which confirmed consignments could move without another booking decision. Maya worked within her authorised category, recording unresolved requests rather than improvising a new form of permission.

Some customers were still disappointed. One could not use the later collection Northline offered and arranged another carrier. Another had to postpone work because a change could not be confirmed in time. The company recorded these consequences and the relevant recovery obligations. A functioning fallback did not make the interruption harmless.

Resilience should be described in units the business can use: which service remains possible, at what volume, for how long and with what loss. “We have a manual process” leaves too much unspecified.

Test what has become unfamiliar

A fallback deteriorates when its dependencies change. The procedure may describe the business before expansion, the person assigned to it may have little recent practice, and the saved record may lack a field needed for the new service, even though each part still appears on a current recovery checklist. Rehearsal needs to join them up.

Rehearsal should expose those differences before a real interruption. It should include an actual attempt to obtain information, allocate authority and complete a limited piece of work without the usual dependency. Reading the procedure aloud can reveal ambiguity; it cannot establish every practical capability.

Northline's earlier exercise had shown that its manual capacity was lower than the normal service. That uncomfortable result became useful now. Sunder did not spend the first hours promising a volume the team had already shown it could not support.

The interruption also revealed something the exercise had not covered adequately: several partners could be impaired at once. The next recovery design would need to account for that shared condition.

Recovery is another consequential change

When the provider returned, the company did not immediately treat every pending request as an accepted instruction. Some customers had made alternative arrangements, some changes had been handled by hand, and replaying the provider's backlog over the top of all that without first reconciling the two accounts could have created a second failure after the outage: duplicate or incompatible commitments, each presented to a customer as confirmed.

Thomas and the service team compared the pending work with the records maintained during the interruption. Sunder confirmed the operating capacity before normal acceptance resumed. The recovery took attention after the screen appeared healthy again.

The screen was healthy before the operation was. Nadia still had requests to answer, Ava had payments to reconcile, and customers had plans that needed to be checked against what the service team had arranged during the interruption; a working screen did not tell any of them which account they could now rely on.

The company could keep using the shared service and the gains it supplied. It did need to decide which dependencies deserved another route, which reduced services it could fund and what exposure it would openly accept. Redundancy has costs too, in money, in maintenance and in the additional complexity of a second route that must be kept working while it is not being used, which is the kind of cost an organisation can pay gladly for one week after an outage and resent quietly for every week after that. The answer should follow the consequence and the available alternatives rather than a general demand to duplicate everything.

Some recovery arrangements must exist between firms

Elise and Peter compared the interruption after ordinary work stabilised. The shared impact had limited the help they could offer one another. Their next agreement included a clearer account of provider dependence and a way to coordinate reduced operations without assuming every participant was healthy.

Other operators using the same arrangements had an interest in the work. No single firm could guarantee continuity for the whole region, and the outage had made that limit visible to the businesses involved, giving them a reason to begin the conversation about common arrangements while the cost of having none was still fresh. They could establish common messages, preserve access to essential records and agree how to identify commitments during a disruption.

By the time Nadia could accept ordinary changes again, one customer had already placed the work elsewhere. Sunder crossed that collection off the pending list. Replaying it would have made the restored system create a new mistake.

28. The Posture

Peter reached the depot while the first vehicles were being prepared. Somebody had left a mug beside the printer. The new labels were coming through without the explanation they used to require.

At the service desk, Maya was examining a proposed extension to the small return-collection test. Thomas had prepared alternatives. Nadia had the customer requests, and Sunder had marked the available capacity. A group of workshops wanted a more dependable way to send suitable items back to suppliers.

Maya pointed to two requests.

“They need the supplier to accept the return first. The collection date isn't the thing holding these up.”

Thomas opened the record. The proposed sequence had assumed acceptance was already in place. This was a draft for an extension, not a booking that had passed the existing acceptance check. Nadia offered to obtain the missing confirmation during her coverage period; Sunder could then examine the collection within the permitted scope. Anything larger would need the board's expansion decision.

Peter had not expressed a view.

The frontier can move

A later system might identify the missing acceptance itself, coordinate the request and complete more of the transaction reliably. The evidence could justify delegating what Maya was doing that morning. Leadership would be poorly founded if it required her to defend the task forever, as though the point of Maya had been the acceptance check rather than the judgment that noticed it was missing, and the judgment would still be hers on the morning the check was automated.

The questions would remain: which work was worth undertaking, whose agreement it required, what means supported the promise and who could challenge its consequences. More capable systems could help answer them, revealing an option people had missed or a cost they had misjudged, while leaving the organisation to choose among purposes whose claims could not all be satisfied by the same resources.

A distributor's dependable priority could consume flexibility a workshop needed. A firm's productive redesign could narrow an employee's acceptable choices. Better reasoning could reveal an arrangement that reduced either conflict; it could not establish that every disagreement arose from somebody's failure to understand. The organisation would need ways to hear claims it could not satisfy as well as errors it could correct.

This is the centre of the leadership I have argued for: find out what is happening without dressing it in language that protects your preferred story, and communicate it simply enough that other people can use and challenge the account. A clear account can support a definite decision while leaving the future uncertain.

Northline had become capable of worthwhile work it once could not afford. It had also failed customers, injured Dennis through an assessment and asked Shaun to accept terms he still disliked. Its repairs mattered because something changed afterwards: the pay record, the funded coverage, the limits on Peter's authority. The company had not acquired a clean history. It had acquired more ways to prevent its preferred version of events from becoming the only one that counted.

Beyond one person's controls

Some of those ways existed between firms. Elise could refuse a request. Both carriers could contest a shared definition. Neither could prepare for their common supplier's failure by assuming the other would remain untouched.

As the scale grows the need for such arrangements grows with it, because many individually sensible plans can combine into damage no participant intended, and widely available capability can sit beside restricted access to the resources needed to use it, leaving even a well-run firm dependent on decisions it cannot make alone. No leader holds all the controls. Recognising that limit is not a counsel of modesty but a direction of effort, towards cooperation with people who can refuse you, standards you did not write, and public institutions whose authority is broader than any private preference, and it is work to undertake now, in the week you have, rather than a reason to postpone everything until a world that will not settle has settled.
