Northline's useful changes began with attempts: a rejected screen, a failed offer, a paid test, a customer's refusal. The team could make another ordinary week better without claiming to know the permanent shape of the economy.

Beyond Northline

Maya has found a missing acceptance. That is a modest ending for a book whose preface asks what happens when problem solving becomes abundant. I want to keep its scale honest: this morning at one firm cannot stand as evidence that the larger world will turn out well.

It can show a way to begin. A useful capability makes a question worth asking; somebody examines it, obtains the necessary agreement and commits enough to learn whether a promise can be kept. Outside the depot, the question might concern a service nobody could afford, an experiment a research team could not justify or a collaboration that had required too much administration to attempt. The same seriousness that prevents a careless promise can make an ambitious one possible.

You do not have to wait until the whole direction is settled to fund a useful attempt, make an explanation accessible, give a colleague time to learn or help an institution hear the person its procedure had missed; those actions can be worthwhile even when the larger forecast remains wrong. Their value has to be found in what they make possible for someone.

I began with fascination, and the qualifications have not removed it. More people able to examine a difficult problem is a large possibility. So is more experience made available across a language, an organisational boundary or a field that previously seemed too distant to enter. I want leaders who can see those openings clearly enough to commit to them, with the money, agreement and patience that useful work asks for.

You will still be finite. Some evenings you will need another person to hold the decision. Some choices will lie beyond your authority. The capability may improve, disappoint, become expensive or answer a question you had not considered. A principle is useful if it helps you decide under those conditions and remain answerable to people who did not choose them.

Take one possibility seriously enough to discover what it would require. Leave the people affected a way to tell you what your account has missed.

At the desk, Nadia had contacted one workshop. Its supplier's acceptance was already available in a separate message. Maya added the fact to the case. The other request remained unresolved.

Sunder could consider the first collection. Thomas brought the existing acceptance check into the proposed extension and kept the missing-acceptance case for its evaluation. The return service still had to earn any broader commitment; the ordinary compact collections were leaving that morning.

Peter asked when they would need a decision from him. They named the condition that would bring the proposal back and the work they could complete themselves.

He went out to the depot floor. Dennis was checking the next consignment against the instructions. Beyond the open door, a vehicle was ready to leave with goods someone had promised to deliver.

Customers we used to turn away may now be worth serving. 18. The Customers You Could Not Afford; Testing complete service economics.

Our pilot works, but the next team or partner still cannot adopt it. 21. First a Tool, Then a Different Business; A forecast that can change a decision.

Different customers are changing at different speeds; we need a forecast. 22. The Uneven Map; A forecast that can change a decision.

We reward a clean number while other people do the hidden repairs. 25. What You Tolerate; Before approving a productivity claim.

An improvement keeps working only because one person rescues it. 26. What Compounds; A recovery you can actually perform.

People still wait for me to settle decisions they should be able to make. 28. The Posture; Delegating a result.

The Principles, Assembled

Return to the chapter when a principle seems too easy to apply. These are aids to recall, not substitutes for its argument, counter-case or consequences.

1. Scarcity Moves, and Value Follows It

Follow a useful outcome to the constraint that still prevents it; distinguish creating value from capturing the proceeds.

2. The Animal at the Controls

Arrange consequential decisions so that evidence can interrupt your preferred account of yourself.

3. What a Master Has Always Been

Earn authority through distinctions that survive examination, including examination of the method that made you important.

4. Wanting

Choose a beneficiary and an outcome clearly enough to refuse competing work.

5. Taste

Train preference against use, not the prestige of the person or process that produced it.

6. Doubt

Spend scrutiny where being wrong changes the decision most.

7. Friction Has a Job

Remove redundant activity while preserving any decision, knowledge or agreement the work still needs.

8. Context, and the Unwritten Why-Not

Give the work access to the reasons behind constraints, including when those reasons should be reconsidered.

9. Asking, Delegating, Stopping

Grant bounded authority, provide a handover someone can receive, and back a sound decision when it becomes costly.

10. Touching the Real Thing

Test the whole promise under the conditions most likely to change your decision.

11. Two Speeds

Lead across the difference between permission to experiment and exposure to consequences.

12. What Happens to a Trade

Analyse the occupation's tasks, demand, bargaining power and entry path separately.

13. Telling the Truth to People

Distinguish what is decided, what remains open, and what support is funded before asking people to rely on reassurance.

14. The Apprentice Problem

Fund the formation of judgment and let the direction of teaching follow the knowledge the work requires.

15. Colleagues, and What Is Left When the Transaction Goes

Give collaboration a real shared purpose instead of assuming incidental dependence will preserve it.

16. Clients, Vendors, and Who Did the Work

Make the promise, relevant method, responsibility and remedy clear enough for an informed agreement.

17. Trust

Match reliance to demonstrated conduct and keep correction available to the person exposed to error.

18. The Customers You Could Not Afford

Revisit rejected demand when its former cost barrier changes, then test the complete economics of serving it.

19. The Ideas You Could Not Afford to Test

Use cheaper search to improve the field of attempts, while investing in a trustworthy way to select and test them.

20. The Organisation You Could Not Afford to Build

Choose the size and boundaries of the organisation around the work it can reliably complete.

21. First a Tool, Then a Different Business

Distinguish access, use, workflow redesign and economic effect; identify the missing complement at each step.

22. The Uneven Map

Forecast the task and its surrounding system, not the prestige of the profession or the sector label.

23. Who Gets the Abundance?

Trace control of the complements and the terms of exchange before inferring who benefits from a technical gain.

24. The Name on the Work

Make the claim behind your name inspectable, then communicate and fund what the affected person can rely on.

25. What You Tolerate

Make rewards, exceptions and consequences tell the same truth as the stated standard.

26. What Compounds

Invest in maintained capabilities that widen future choices for the institution and its people.

27. What Breaks

Build recovery around capacities you can actually exercise and dependencies you can name.

28. The Posture

Stay ambitious about what can become possible, exact about what is known, and willing to be corrected by people who bear the consequences.

Working Pages

These pages are places to begin an inquiry. Use them when they help you make a decision clearer. A completed page is not evidence that the decision is good, and some of the people affected may see something the page does not ask about.

Write in ordinary language. If a colleague cannot tell what you intend to do, replace the label with the action. Keep confidential material within the arrangements that apply to your work. Do not place it in an external tool merely because a worksheet invites you to record it.

Before approving a productivity claim

Choose one claim your organisation is making about an improvement. Work through it from the recipient's need to the delivered result.

The useful outcome. What can a customer, colleague or beneficiary now do? “More documents” describes output. “A customer receives a confirmed collection without making a second call” identifies a result someone can examine.

The comparison. What happened before, and under which conditions? Compare like work where possible. Record what else changed: customer mix, workload, staffing, service scope or the amount of informal repair.

The released resource. Did the change release paid time, avoid an actual expense, improve quality, increase capacity or permit new work? More than one answer may be true. Keep their accounts separate.

The next constraint. Where does the additional work now wait? What would you invest in next if the claimed gain were real? What would you stop funding?

The hidden contribution. Who corrects errors, maintains context, explains confusing results or supports the system? Give that work a place in the account.

The allocation. What will happen to the released capacity? Name an owner and an observable result. If several projects claim the same hours, the account is not yet reconciled.

The gain and its distribution. Who receives lower cost, better service, income, time or additional responsibility? Who can negotiate the terms? A gain to the firm does not establish a gain to every participant.

End with a sentence you could say to the team: “We have evidence of this improvement, we have not established this further claim, and we are using the gain for this purpose.”

A decision while the facts are incomplete

Write the decision as an action with a scope: approve a limited trial, commit to a service, change a role, or stop an activity. Avoid beginning with the argument for your preferred answer.

Then record four things separately:

  • What you have observed, with its source and relevant conditions.
  • What you infer from it.
  • What you want to happen.
  • What you fear will happen if you wait.

The separation may reveal that the question you are asking is already shaped around a desired outcome. That does not make the desire illegitimate. It makes its role visible.

Choose the uncertain assumption most likely to reverse the decision. Describe an observation that would test it. If the observation would not change what you do, explain why it is worth obtaining. Sometimes a test is required for reasons beyond the immediate decision; sometimes it is simply postponement.

Specify the commitment that must be made before the answer is available. Can it be narrowed? What cannot readily be undone? Who bears the cost of finding out, and what authority do you have to ask them to bear it?

Keep the original account. When the result arrives, compare it with what you expected before explaining it. A decision record earns its value when it makes revision possible, including revision of a successful decision whose reasoning was poor.

Delegating a result

Use this page before giving a person or a system meaningful discretion. The language may be simple even when the underlying work is complex.

Result: What must be true when the work is complete? Who will use it?

Context: Which current facts and constraints matter? Where are they maintained? Which information is missing or uncertain?

Authority: What may the delegate decide or change? What commitment requires another person's approval? A useful suggestion must not become a purchase, message or booking simply because the interface permits it.

Evidence: What makes completion observable? Which checks are proportionate to the possible consequences? If someone must review the work, do they have the competence, time and information to do so?

Stop: Which condition ends the authority to continue? What happens to partially completed work? Who receives the unresolved matter, and how will they know it is theirs?

Recovery: If the action is wrong, what can be corrected, by whom and at whose expense? Test a concrete example rather than writing “revert if necessary.”

Learning: What record would help improve the next attempt without retaining unnecessary personal or sensitive information?

Add a latest useful decision time, an acknowledged recipient and named cover if that person is absent. State which previous commitment remains valid while the case waits.

Try the arrangement on an awkward case. If every exception returns to a person who cannot respond, the stop rule has moved the failure rather than handled it.

A transition and consultation promise

Begin with the change to work, pay, hours, location, authority or prospects. Do not begin with a message about how much the organisation values its people.

Separate the facts into three groups: decided, open to influence, and not yet known. For each open matter, identify who can change it and when the opportunity to influence it closes. Do not call a meeting consultation if all consequential choices are already fixed.

For each proposed support, record what exists behind the words. A course needs a place, paid time where promised, relevant teaching and a plausible use for the learning. A new role needs actual work, terms, selection criteria and a person authorised to offer it. A financial promise needs funding.

Ask what the recipient needs to decide. They may need written terms, time to consider, a representative, an accessible explanation or a private conversation. The leader's preference for a quick, reassuring meeting should not determine the whole process.

Write the sentence you are most tempted to soften. Then make it accurate and understandable without making it needlessly harsh. “We cannot currently offer an equivalent daytime role” is more useful than language that implies continuity while leaving the person to discover otherwise.

Finish with the actual hours, rate, weekly pay, duration and start date of any proposed terms, plus the funded handover and next conversation. A change from five days to four at the same rate still reduces weekly pay. Record the person’s disagreement without converting it into consent.

After the conversation, record what you now understand that the original plan omitted. A truthful communication is not finished when the leader's prepared words have been delivered.

Designing an entry role and learning path

Choose a capability someone needs to develop. Describe it through a situation: recognising when a familiar method no longer applies, diagnosing an unfamiliar failure, or explaining a commitment to a customer who challenges it.

Find work that exposes the relevant distinction. The most difficult task is not necessarily the best first task. The learner needs enough responsibility to encounter consequences and enough support to keep the early mistakes recoverable.

Agree on what assistance is useful and what the learner needs to demonstrate. If independent performance matters, explain why it matters in that role. If the normal work properly includes a tool, assess competent use of that tool as well. Do not make unaided performance a ceremony detached from the job.

Ask the learner to state an expectation before seeing the outcome. Afterwards, discuss what happened and which part of the expectation needs revision. Use a new case to distinguish understanding from memory of the previous answer.

Budget the teacher's time. Decide which work moves to make it available, how teaching receives credit and who takes over when the teacher is absent. If the plan relies on a conscientious expert quietly donating evenings, it has not yet been funded.

Write a progression another supervisor can use: observe these cases; attempt this limited decision with cover; show transfer on an unfamiliar case; receive this wider authority. Name an alternate supervisor and the work removed from each teacher’s schedule.

Finally, ask what evidence of capability the learner can carry elsewhere. A learning relationship should increase someone's ability to act, not merely their dependence on one institution's approval.

A forecast that can change a decision

Choose a consequential development you expect: customers moving to a new way of buying, an activity becoming economical to automate, or a supplier acquiring greater power.

Write the mechanism. “AI is improving” is too broad. Say which capability matters, what else must become available and why someone has an incentive to change.

Name the counterforces. They might include the cost of error, inaccessible information, physical investment, professional duties, unwilling customers or a supplier's terms. These are not reasons to assume nothing will happen. They are conditions that influence what happens next.

Identify a few observations that would move your own action. What would make you invest sooner? What would make you defer? What would make the proposed opportunity disappear? Keep the observation distinct from the action: widespread experimentation may justify learning without justifying a large commitment.

Put a date on evidence when its age matters. A study from a particular year and task remains evidence about that setting. It should not quietly become a current description of every workplace.

Revisit the forecast when a relevant condition changes. Keep the earlier version. A forecast becomes a useful leadership instrument when it improves a choice, not when its author can continually rewrite it to appear prescient.

A recovery you can actually perform

Choose one dependency your organisation relies on: a provider, a data source, a piece of infrastructure or a person with uncommon knowledge. Imagine it becomes unavailable during ordinary work.

Describe the reduced service you could provide. Specify the volume, duration and work you would have to decline. Name the records, skills and permissions needed to operate that way. Check whether they remain available when the dependency is gone.

Look beyond your own organisation. Do the supposed alternatives use the same underlying provider? Would partners be trying to obtain the same limited fallback capacity? Agreement among several tools can be one shared assumption speaking several times.

Rehearse a modest part of the recovery within the authority and obligations of your setting. Record what could actually be done and what existed only in the plan. Change the promise to match the capacity, or invest in the capacity before expanding the promise.

Before normal operation resumes, compare pending requests, accepted commitments and actions taken during the interruption. Assign someone to resolve duplicates and conflicts before replaying queued work. Restoration of a provider is not confirmation that every pending action remains wanted.

Choose what to maintain afterwards. A fallback that nobody can perform next year is a record of a former capability. Reliability includes the work of keeping a less impressive service available when the impressive one fails.

Challenging an assessment

Start with the consequence, not the score: a lost assignment, changed pay, restricted access or an adverse record. Identify when the next consequence will occur.

Give the affected person access to the basis: relevant inputs, comparison group, definitions, period and missing context, with an explanation they can use. Name a reviewer who can change the result and the date by which the review will affect the pending decision.

Decide interim treatment explicitly. Will the disputed result continue to operate, be suspended or be replaced by another measure? State why and who bears the risk. “Under review” is inadequate when a flag is still excluding someone.

Finish with a repair record: what changed, who received the original claim and needs the correction, which pay or opportunity was lost, what remedy is authorised and how the next challenge can be raised. Dennis's corrected number did not by itself restore two weeks of paid responsibility or the experience he missed.

Testing complete service economics

Write the promise first: who receives what, how often, within which limits, and what is excluded. Choose a period over which both revenue and the work required can be inspected.

Build an account with collected or credible revenue, costs that vary with volume, capacity that must be reserved, paid administration and support, expected recovery, and an explicit share of wider costs. Keep initial setup and working-capital needs separate from the recurring account. Record unpaid or borrowed effort at the cost needed to sustain it.

Northline's compact weekly example at 28 customers is $3,360 revenue less $2,780 defined cost: $580 contribution. Allocating $300 to wider costs leaves $280. A further $400 recovery expense turns that into a loss of $120. The separate $4,800 setup allowance has not vanished because the weekly account is positive.

“Positive at 28, therefore launch at 32” is an inadequate conclusion. Identify the capacity assumption that could fail as volume or exception mix changes. End with an approved scope, the adverse case you can absorb, the condition that stops expansion and the next evidence needed. Contribution is not whole-company profit.

Removing a workflow step or managerial activity

Take one recent instance, not the meeting's official purpose. What information moved? Which conflict was settled, condition noticed, person taught or commitment authorised? Ask a recipient what they would have had to do without it.

For each function, choose: no longer needed; supplied elsewhere; or needs a replacement. A shared view may replace a status call while leaving the priority decision homeless. Give that decision a route before cancelling the call.

Name the people whose work changes and conduct a bounded removal. Watch where unresolved cases, repair work and delayed customer decisions appear. If these worsen, repair the missing function; do not automatically restore the whole meeting.

The output is a short removal decision: “We stop this activity, retain this function through this arrangement, and examine these consequences after this period.” It should explain why somebody can safely remove the recurring invitation.

Approving readiness or a larger scope

Put the tested promise beside the proposed promise. Compare customers, locations, timing, volume, exception mix, suppliers and response capacity. Circle every condition the earlier result did not establish.

Obtain an operating account from the people expected to perform the work and a financial account that includes repair. They need time to inspect and the right to state an unmet condition. State who holds the launch decision; several signatures do not decide it by themselves.

A useful readiness entry says: “Ordinary handovers at fixed sites worked; changes between listed sites still require a timed acceptance test with both carriers.” “Handover proven” is too broad for that decision.

End with the next authorised scope and any conditions that remain unmet. Record an attractive opportunity declined under the limit as well as the launches it allows. Reconsider when the missing operating evidence exists, not merely when the commercial deadline becomes uncomfortable.

Deciding who receives a gain

Keep three accounts: who can now use the capability; what benefit it creates; and who retains money or other valued advantages. Set a period for each observation. A customer may gain reliable service while the provider's margin remains small.

List the claims on the benefit: the people who created it, the resources needed to sustain it, losses imposed elsewhere and commitments already made. Examine who has alternatives, who controls access to customers or infrastructure and what switching actually costs.

Compare a small number of concrete allocations. State what each displaces. Rebuilding a recovery reserve, improving terms for workers and lowering prices cannot all spend the same money. Distinguish a one-time distribution from a recurring pay commitment.

Finish with the allocation, the person or body authorised to decide it, matters requiring negotiation and a review trigger. Give affected people the account and a route to dispute it. If the answer depends on wider bargaining rules or shared institutions, identify the arrangement you would support and the authority you do not possess. A request for patience should name what would end the wait.

Under pressure

Use these three questions to state the immediate decision in thirty seconds. Existing emergency procedures and qualified authority take precedence.

  1. What must be protected now? Name the person, commitment or safe condition at risk, and the point after which harm becomes harder to prevent.
  2. What can we reliably do with the people and information available? Keep the next action within known authority and capacity. State the critical fact still missing.
  3. Who owns the next decision, and by when? Obtain acknowledgment. Tell the person waiting what remains in force and when the next answer will come.

If the conditions change

Take one proposed commitment. Write the capability, cost and customer behaviour it assumes. Record the money, time and obligations you would find hardest to recover.

First test acceleration: if the capability becomes dependable at a task your plan assumes it cannot do, what would you stop defending and what better attempt would you fund? Name the evidence that would justify changing scope. Improvement does not by itself authorise a larger promise.

Then complete the three columns below. Use a sentence per answer, with a named owner where the response needs action.

The capability stalls The price changes materially The direction surprises you
Which part of the plan needs an improvement not yet demonstrated? Which part needs today's price or terms to continue? Which part needs customers to keep solving the problem in the same way?
What would you stop funding or promising at the present capability? What would you stop, reprice or move after counting transition costs? What would you stop if the transaction or need changed?
What useful work and competence would you keep? What service could you still sustain, and through which available route? What useful capability would remain relevant to the changed need?
Who needs the first revised account: team, customer, partner or funder? Who needs notice before you alter a price, promise or supplier? Who can tell you that demand has changed, and who needs your response?

Finish with the observation that would trigger each response, who will watch for it and the last useful date for deciding. Revisit the record when the evidence changes. The purpose is to expose a dependence before it becomes an obligation someone else cannot escape.

Technical Background and Opening Notes

You do not need to build a model to read this book. You do need to distinguish a few things that the same conversational interface can make look identical.

A language model is trained by adjusting numerical parameters to improve its performance on an objective. For models trained to predict text, the objective concerns the next token—a piece of text, sometimes a word and sometimes part of one. The result is a system whose learned patterns can support many tasks. In the GPT-3 research, for example, instructions and examples supplied in text elicited different kinds of performance without updating the model's parameters for each task.[2]

That is different from consulting a perfectly indexed copy of everything in the training material. It is also different from learning a fact about Northline this morning. The model may need that fact supplied in its present context or obtained through a connected source. In our story, knowing how delivery businesses generally work will not reveal that a particular driver is absent.

Training can continue after an initial model is built. One influential research approach used demonstrations and human preferences to improve how a language model followed instructions. The researchers also reported that mistakes remained.[3] A fluent, helpful conversational manner therefore should not be mistaken for a separate guarantee of correctness. Nor should we assume that every system uses the same training recipe.

The possibility of learned internal representations is more than a philosophical question. Researchers studying a model trained on sequences of Othello moves found evidence of an internal representation of the board state, including experiments that changed the model's output by intervening on that representation.[4] That is evidence in a controlled game setting. It is not evidence that a general assistant possesses a complete or consistently usable account of a business, a person or the world.

Finally, a model can be placed inside a larger system that retrieves information and takes actions. Research such as ReAct explored alternating reasoning and interaction with external sources or environments.[5] An application that can inspect a booking record or change a schedule has different practical consequences from one that can only suggest a reply. Its behaviour depends on the model, the information supplied, the tools and the permissions around them.

These distinctions give a leader better questions. Was the necessary fact available? Did the system use it correctly? Did a suggested action become a commitment without the required check? Did the test resemble the work being authorised? An impressive answer to one of those questions does not answer the others.

The capabilities may improve substantially. The need to establish what a particular system can do in a particular situation remains. That is a basis for competent ambition: find out what the tool makes possible, then build the conditions in which the possibility becomes useful.

Sources

  1. The interpretation of learned representations in the preface is deliberately provisional. Ilya Sutskever's 2023 interview with Dwarkesh Patel offers one researcher's argument connecting prediction with understanding. It does not settle the reliability or completeness of a particular system's representations. Northline and all its workplace details are fiction.
  2. Tom B. Brown and colleagues, Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, 2020. The distinction between training and use of examples in context follows the paper's specified evaluation approach; its historical benchmark results are not a description of today's entire market.
  3. Long Ouyang and colleagues, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, 2022. This is one documented training approach, not a universal architecture or a guarantee that user intent is always followed.
  4. Kenneth Li and colleagues, Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task, first posted 2022, presented at ICLR 2023, revised 2024. The example is specifically a model trained on Othello sequences.
  5. Shunyu Yao and colleagues, ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, first posted 2022, ICLR version 2023. The reference illustrates connecting reasoning and actions; no benchmark result is taken as a general deployment guarantee.

About the author

Rahul Kapil is a data and machine-learning practitioner with experience building learning systems and algorithms for technology companies. He holds a Bachelor of Technology degree from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

His interests include information theory, game theory, decision-making under uncertainty, complex systems, microeconomics, psychology and ancient Vedic wisdom. The AI Native Leader brings his practical experience and curiosity to a question that reaches beyond technology: what happens to work and leadership when problem-solving capability becomes widely available?
